@@135889435 <p> New research sheds light on an often-overlooked threat to groundwater : naturally occurring fluoride contamination . While fluoride at low levels can benefit dental health , excessive concentrations pose serious risks , particularly in regions where water monitoring systems are limited . A growing body of research now shows that artificial intelligence ( AI ) can play a critical role in identifying and managing these risks at scale . <p> The study highlights a critical global challenge : fluoride contamination is often geogenic , meaning it originates from natural geological processes rather than human pollution . This makes it harder to detect and manage , particularly in regions where water quality testing is infrequent or infrastructure is limited . By integrating hydrochemical data with machine learning , researchers are now able to map contamination risks with greater accuracy and provide actionable insights for policymakers . <h> Machine learning enables scalable detection of groundwater risks <p> The study shows how machine learning can enhance groundwater monitoring . Traditional approaches rely heavily on physical sampling , which is often expensive , time-consuming , and geographically limited . As a result , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ populations exposed to unseen risks . <p> The research shows that machine learning models can bridge this gap by using available water chemistry data to predict contamination patterns across larger areas . Among the models tested , the Support Vector Classifier proved particularly effective in distinguishing between safe and contaminated water sources , achieving strong predictive performance when applied to spatially diverse conditions . <p> By analyzing key hydrochemical indicators such as pH , electrical conductivity , total dissolved solids , and concentrations of major ions , the model captures the complex interactions that influence fluoride levels in groundwater . These variables act as proxies for underlying geological processes , allowing the model to infer contamination risks even in areas where direct measurements are unavailable . <p> The resulting spatial risk maps provide a powerful tool for decision-making . Instead of relying on scattered data points , authorities can identify high-risk zones , prioritize testing and treatment efforts , and allocate resources more efficiently . In the Pakistan case study , several localities were identified as high-risk , illustrating how such models can pinpoint vulnerable communities with precision . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , where groundwater serves as the main drinking water source , the ability to predict contamination risks without extensive fieldwork could significantly improve water safety and reduce public health burdens . <h> Natural geological processes drive fluoride contamination <p> Fluoride contamination is largely driven by natural geological conditions rather than industrial or agricultural pollution . This has important implications for how the problem is understood and addressed . <p> Fluoride enters groundwater through the dissolution of minerals such as fluorite and other fluoride-bearing rocks . This process is influenced by factors including water chemistry , temperature , and the length of time water remains in contact with geological formations . In regions with alkaline conditions and high mineral content , fluoride is more likely to accumulate in groundwater . <p> According to the study , higher fluoride concentrations are often associated with elevated levels of dissolved solids and specific ions such as sodium and bicarbonate . These indicators point to prolonged water-rock interaction , which increases the likelihood of fluoride release . <p> This geogenic origin makes fluoride contamination fundamentally different from many other water quality issues . While pollution @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ management , naturally occurring contaminants require different strategies , such as water treatment , alternative water sourcing , or blending of water supplies . <p> The findings underscore the importance of integrating geological knowledge into water management practices . Without an understanding of the underlying processes , efforts to address contamination may be ineffective or misdirected . <h> Children face higher health risks from fluoride exposure <p> The study also provides a detailed assessment of human health risks associated with fluoride exposure . The results reveal a concerning trend : children are significantly more vulnerable to the effects of contaminated water than adults . <p> Using hazard quotient analysis , the researchers found that a substantial proportion of water sources exceed safe exposure levels for children . In the Pakistan case study , more than half of the sampled locations posed potential health risks for younger populations , while the proportion was considerably lower for adults . <p> This disparity is linked to differences in body weight , water consumption rates , and physiological sensitivity . Children 's developing bones and teeth are particularly susceptible to excessive fluoride , increasing @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The findings highlight the need for targeted public health interventions . In many regions , awareness of fluoride risks remains low , and communities may continue to use contaminated water without realizing the potential consequences . Schools , healthcare providers , and local authorities play a critical role in educating populations and promoting safer water practices . <p> The study also emphasizes the value of integrating health risk assessments with environmental monitoring . By linking contamination data with potential health outcomes , policymakers can better understand the urgency of the issue and design more effective responses . <h> Toward smarter and more sustainable groundwater management <p> The broader significance of the research lies in its potential to inform global water management strategies . As climate change , population growth , and urbanization place increasing pressure on water resources , ensuring the safety of groundwater supplies has become a critical priority . <p> The integration of AI into environmental monitoring represents a major step forward . Machine learning models can process large datasets , identify patterns , and generate predictions that would be difficult to achieve through traditional methods @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ resources , where efficient use of data can make a significant difference . <p> However , the study also highlights the need for a comprehensive approach that combines technology with policy and community engagement . While predictive models can identify risks , addressing those risks requires investment in infrastructure , such as water treatment systems and alternative supply sources . <p> Regulatory frameworks must also evolve to incorporate new technologies and ensure that water quality standards are effectively enforced . In addition , international collaboration is essential , as fluoride contamination is a shared challenge affecting multiple regions . <p> The case study from Pakistan serves as a clear example of how localized research can generate insights with global relevance . Similar conditions exist in many parts of the world , including regions of India , China , Africa , and the Middle East , where geological factors contribute to elevated fluoride levels in groundwater . By applying the methodologies demonstrated in this study , these regions can improve their understanding of contamination patterns and develop more effective management strategies .

Across India , snakebite deaths have more than doubled from 183 in 2023 to 431 in 2025 , but Karnataka 's rise has been particularly sharp . @@135890444 <p> Srinagar , Apr 01 : The widening of the Srinagar-Baramulla-Uri highway has led to the diversion of over 20 hectares of forest land and the felling of 740 trees , the Jammu and Kashmir government informed the Assembly on Wednesday . According to the government , a total of 20.9352 hectares of forest land has been diverted for the construction of the Srinagar-Baramulla-Uri Road ( Section-4 ) , executed by the Border Roads Organisation ( BRO ) <p> in Baramulla district under the Forest Conservation Act , 1980 . Final clearance for the diversion was granted by the Ministry of Environment , Forest and Climate Change . The Minister further informed that 740 forest trees were affected , including 623 poles ( 30 -- 90 cm girth ) and 117 fully grown trees ( above 90 cm girth ) . Regarding compensation , the government said the executing agency @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ diversion . This includes Rs 96.43 lakh for compensatory afforestation and Rs 2.87 crore as Net Present Value ( NPV ) of the diverted forest land . Compensatory afforestation is being carried out over degraded forest land at three sites : Kitcharma <p> Forest in Baramulla , Mond Forest in Doabgah , and Khahmoh area under the Jammu and Kashmir Forest Department . The government also disclosed that a plantation plan involving 27,000 saplings over 27 hectares was completed during 2024 -- 25 . No fresh plantation target has been set for 2026 as afforestation work under the project stands completed . On ecological safeguards , the Minister stated that the BRO has undertaken slope stabilization and restoration measures along the affected highway stretch , including the construction of breast walls and retaining walls at vulnerable locations . Against a planned length of 22,315 metres , around 15,900 metres of such works have already been completed .

They also measured how population size has historically aligned with changes in climate , emissions , and the ecological footprint to understand how human numbers cause environmental stress.The study found that before the 1950s , global population growth actually sped up as human abundance increased . More people meant more innovation , more energy use , and more rapid technological development that supported further expansion.However , this pattern broke down in the early 1960s when the global growth rate began to fall even as the population continued to rise . " This shift marked the beginning of what we call ' a negative demographic phase , ' " says Professor Bradshaw . " It means that adding more people no longer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , we found the global population is likely to peak somewhere between 11.7 and 12.4 billion people by the late 2060s or 2070s if current trends hold . " Professor Bradshaw says this upper limit is dangerous and has only been possible to date because human societies have relied on fossil fuels and drained natural resources faster than nature can replace them . " The truly sustainable population is much lower and closer to what the world supported in the mid-twentieth century . Our calculations show a sustainable global population closer to about 2.5 billion people if everyone were to live within ecological limits and comfortable , economically secure living standards , " he says.The researchers say the enormous gap between that sustainable number and today 's population of now 8.3 billion highlights the scale of global overconsumption . They argue that this overshoot has been hidden for decades by heavy reliance on fossil fuels , which boosted food production , energy supply , and industry , but also accelerated climate change and pollution.The study shows a strong link between increasing population size and rising global temperatures , larger ecological @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Total population size explained more variation in these environmental indicators than per-capita consumption.Professor Bradshaw says this highlights how both human numbers and consumption patterns jointly intensify environmental stress . " Humanity 's current path will push societies into deeper crises unless we make major changes , " he says . Our study shows these limits are not theoretical but unfolding right now . @@135922105 <p> In Japan , the delicate blossoms of the cherry tree bear the weight of a storied history and a $9-billion tourism industry . For a few days every year , millions of people -- Japanese and visitors -- gather in gardens and parks around the country to contemplate the brief beauty of the sakura . The stakes are high , hinging on a deceptively simple question : When will the flowers bloom ? As the long-established system of answering this question , determined by weather reports , is destabilised by climate change , forecasters increasingly depend on artificial intelligence to honour the tradition of hanami , or flower viewing . <p> Perhaps there is something ironic about attempting to pin down a tradition , the essence of which is an acknowledgement - -- and celebration -- of evanescence . The 72 micro-seasons ( shichijuni ko ) into which the Japanese calendar was once divided invited a more intimate relationship with the world , based on subtle changes in nature . Seasons like " fish emerge from the ice " ( mid-February ) and " crickets chirp around the door @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crop calendar and inspired poets . They governed the fine variations in how tea was prepared from one week to the next and influenced how a garden evolved over the course of a year . Today , Japan may follow the Gregorian calendar like the rest of the world , but sensibilities -- aesthetic and cultural -- continue to be shaped by an older rhythm . <p> Advertisement <p> " This is the real pleasure/ of this life without tomorrow/ The flowers , the sake , " wrote the 19th century haiku master , Inoue Seigetsu . Today , when time is increasingly measured by the beeps of devices and app notifications , rituals like the hanami are a portal into a world where time marches to a slower beat . And if the most cutting-edge technology can open that door a little wider , a little more reliably , so be it .

@@135922454 <h> The gap between reported and felt inflation is about to widen : RBI should take note <p> With domestic supply shocks from adverse climate events piling onto fuel shocks , even as the headline inflation rate rises , perceived inflation will be even higher . ( PTI ) <p> Summary <p> India 's reworked consumer price index is an upgrade , but its weight for cooking gas being under 2% means an LPG price spike will barely register in headline inflation . Public perceptions of price instability are sure to diverge from official readings . <p> On 12 March , when February inflation printed at 3.2% , the war in West Asia had been raging for 13 days . Oil company retail agencies , which sell cylinders of liquefied petroleum gas ( LPG ) at an administered price to registered users , shuttered their doors , anticipating supply cuts . <p> Consumers were forced to turn to the informal market , where the price had risen five-fold by 12 March , relative to the regulated price even without the Ujjwala price subsidy . Retail agencies later re-opened to long @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ gap between the official inflation rate and the fuel price spike . This kind of dissonance between reported and experienced inflation is intrinsic to the nature of a single inflation rate , which is a weighted average over a diverse array of consumable goods and services . @@135923898 <p> A unique election campaign is unfolding in Puthuppally , arguably the most closely watched constituency in Kerala 's forthcoming Assembly elections . It is unique because it lacks the pomp and show usually associated with traditional poll campaigns . <p> Elections have always announced themselves in Puthuppally long before political parties finalised their candidates . Like elsewhere in the state , they arrived in waves of material . Massive plastic flex boards tied to trees , banners stretched across junctions , vinyl sheets nailed into public spaces , and loudspeakers mounted on vehicles cutting through villages from dawn to dusk . Campaigns did not merely communicate . They accumulated , layer upon layer , until the constituency itself became an archive of political assertion . When it ended , what remained was not just a result but a residue . Waste to be cleared , plastic to be managed , and a landscape marked by the physical imprint of democracy . <p> But this time , there are no flex boards crowding Puthuppally 's busy but narrow junctions announcing the presence of UDF candidate Chandy Oommen . There are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ amplifying his voice . <p> Instead , there is a 37-year-old lawyer , the son of former chief minister Oommen Chandy , moving through the constituency on a bicycle , stopping at homes , speaking without a microphone , and leaving nothing to be cleared . It is a campaign defined as much by what it refuses to do as by what it chooses to become . <h> A ' green campaign ' <p> Oommen 's " green campaign " is not an abstract environmental gesture . It is a direct intervention in Kerala 's political culture . <p> The contradiction is stark . Regulations exist , but compliance is sporadic . Sustainability is spoken about , but rarely practised . Across political fronts , campaigns still rely heavily on plastic , visual saturation , and high-decibel outreach , often treating environmental norms as procedural hurdles rather than political commitments . <p> It is against this backdrop of routine excess that Oommen 's campaign gains its significance . " What Chandy is doing in Puthuppally is a quiet revolution that deserves to be emulated across the country . At a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ boards , it is rare in Kerala for a young candidate to decide that none of this is necessary to communicate his politics , and that environmental commitment must go beyond hollow statements to become a way of life . He is also sending out the message that ecological alternatives must emerge from the grassroots , " writer and political observer Sudha Menon told Down To Earth . <p> Her observation points to a shift from symbolism to practice . What distinguishes this campaign is not that it speaks about sustainability , but that it attempts to embody it . The absence of flex boards is not replaced by digital spectacle or another form of excess . Instead , the campaign reorients itself around proximity . Door-to-door visits , small conversations , and a pace that allows interruption . Even Rahul Gandhi , who arrived to campaign for Oommen , took note of the approach and joined him on a bicycle through the constituency . <p> The bicycle becomes central to this reimagining . It is not merely an environmentally friendly choice . It alters the rhythm of politics . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ remains accessible , exposed to the everyday life of the constituency . Conversations happen not as staged events but as encounters . Brief , unscripted , and grounded in local concerns . In a political culture increasingly defined by scale and speed , this slowing down becomes both method and message . <p> Menon reads this as part of a broader transition . " What he is demonstrating is a compelling model for change , especially in how we think about transport and everyday mobility . It speaks to multiple crises at once : climate change , traffic congestion , public health , and even the erosion of local social connections . By choosing a different path , he is showing that political practice itself can become a site of meaningful change , " she says . <p> The environmental dimension is reinforced by another significant decision , the refusal to use plastic banners and hoardings . For Thiruvananthapuram-based environmental activist S Usha , this marks a break from the habitual disconnect between political messaging and political practice . People have always fought with each other . Archaeologists have discovered skeletons with weapon injuries that are over 10,000 years old . <p> Wars are very serious because they hurt people and the environment . They happen for many different reasons , and each war is different . People who start wars often think that the short-term benefits of a war are worth the harm to their own people . But they do n't always understand the long-term consequences of their actions . <p> Experts use something called the " just war theory " to understand whether it 's ever OK to fight a war . The rules say that normal people and the things that they need , such as hospitals , power plants and schools , should never be attacked because they help everyone live safely . <p> These ancient ideas have become part of the modern international laws and agreements that help make our world more peaceful . <p> Unfortunately , not all countries follow ' just war ' theory when they go to war . @@135924292 <h> Future Foods : Exploring Novel Food Products for Better Nutrition <p> Introduction : Food is not only a basic necessity for survival but also a key factor in maintaining health and well-being . In recent years , rapid population growth , climate change , urbanization , and changing lifestyles have created new challenges for the global food system . Traditional food sources alone are no longer sufficient to meet the increasing demand for nutritious , safe , and sustainable food . As a result , the concept of " future foods " has emerged , focusing on innovative and novel food products that can ensure better nutrition for present and future generations . <p> Future foods are not just about new ingredients ; they represent a shift toward smarter , healthier , and more sustainable eating patterns . These foods aim to address issues like malnutrition , food insecurity , and environmental sustainability while catering to modern consumer preferences . <p> What are Future Foods ? Future foods refer to innovative , sustainable , and nutritionally enhanced food products developed using modern science , technology , and traditional knowledge @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ plant-based products , and functional foods designed to improve health outcomes . <p> Need for Future FoodsThe need for future foods arises from several global and local challenges . First , the world population is expected to reach nearly 10 billion by 2050 , increasing pressure on food production systems . <p> Second , malnutrition remains a serious issue , especially in developing countries like India , where deficiencies of iron , protein , and vitamins are common . Additionally , modern diets often rely heavily on processed foods that are high in fats , sugar , and salt , leading to lifestyle diseases such as obesity , diabetes , and heart disease . <p> Types of Future Foods1 . Millet-Based ProductsMillets are traditional grains that are now gaining popularity as " superfoods . " They are rich in fiber , minerals , and antioxidants . Products like millet cookies , pancakes , noodles , and ready-to-eat snacks are being developed to make millets more appealing to consumers . Millets are drought-resistant and require less water , making them environmentally sustainable . They are especially beneficial for managing diabetes and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ becoming a major trend worldwide . These include products made from soy , peas , lentils , and chickpeas that serve as alternatives to meat and dairy . Plant-based milk , tofu , and meat substitutes are gaining popularity due to their health benefits and lower environmental impact . These foods are rich in protein , cholesterol-free , and suitable for vegetarians and vegans . <p> 4 . Bio-fortified FoodsBiofortification is the process of increasing the nutritional value of crops through breeding or biotechnology . Examples include iron-rich rice , zinc-enriched wheat , and vitamin A-rich sweet potatoes . Such foods are particularly important in addressing micronutrient deficiencies in rural populations . <p> 5 . Insect-Based FoodsAlthough not widely accepted in India , insect-based foods are considered a sustainable protein source globally . Insects like crickets and mealworms are rich in protein , vitamins , and minerals and require fewer resources to produce . <p> 6 . Algae and Seaweed-Based FoodsAlgae and seaweed are nutrient-dense foods rich in proteins , vitamins , and antioxidants . They are used in making supplements , snacks , and functional beverages . <p> These @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ impact . <p> Role of Technology in Future FoodsModern technology plays a crucial role in the development of future foods . Techniques such as food processing , preservation , biotechnology , and nanotechnology help improve the quality , safety , and nutritional value of food products . <p> For example : * 3D food printing can create customized foods * Artificial intelligence helps in food formulation and quality control * Cold chain technology improves shelf life Technology also enables the development of ready-to-eat and convenience foods , which are in high demand due to busy lifestyles . <p> Challenges and LimitationsDespite their advantages , future foods face several challenges : * Consumer Acceptance : People may hesitate to try new or unfamiliar foods * Cost : Some novel foods are expensive to produce * Lack of Awareness : Limited knowledge among consumers * Regulatory Issues : Need for proper safety and quality standards To overcome these challenges , awareness programs , training , and government support are essential . <p> ConclusionFuture foods represent a transformative approach to addressing the nutritional and environmental challenges of the modern world . By combining @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , nutritious , and innovative solutions for better health . <p> Promoting future foods is not just a scientific necessity but also a social responsibility . @@135941495 <h> Proximity Without Opportunity : Rethinking the 15-Minute City in India <h> Published on Apr 02 , 2026 <p> The 15-minute city prioritises proximity , but in India , the real urban challenge lies not in access to local amenities , but in unequal access to jobs , quality services , and efficient mobility across the city <p> Image Source : Pixabay <p> The ' 15-minute city ' concept , popularised by Carlos Moreno and widely adopted in Paris , has rapidly become a dominant narrative in global urban planning discourse . Promoted as a solution to climate change , congestion , and the decline in the quality of urban life , the idea has been widely embraced and rebranded under labels such as " complete communities " and " walkable neighbourhoods . " Yet its growing popularity warrants closer scrutiny , particularly in contexts far removed from the cities where it was first championed . <p> At its core , the 15-minute city proposes that residents should be able to access essential daily needs such as housing , work , healthcare , education , commerce , and recreation within @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ principles of proximity , low-carbon accessibility , and multifunctional land use , Moreno 's vision seeks to foster social cohesion , reduce dependence on private vehicles , and promote healthier , pedestrian-oriented lifestyles . <p> While Indian cities may resemble 15-minute cities in form , they differ markedly in function . The central challenge lies not in access to amenities , but in access to opportunity , particularly employment , and the deep spatial inequities that shape urban life . <p> However , when applied to Indian cities , the promise of the 15-minute city becomes more ambiguous . Many Indian neighbourhoods already display the density , compactness , and mixed-use characteristics that the model aspires to create . Daily services are often close at hand , supported by extensive informal economies . Yet this apparent alignment is misleading . While Indian cities may resemble 15-minute cities in form , they differ markedly in function . The central challenge lies not in access to amenities , but in access to opportunity , particularly employment , and the deep spatial inequities that shape urban life . <p> The critical question , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as 15-minute cities , but whether the concept meaningfully addresses the realities of labour markets , affordability , and inequality that define Indian urbanisation . <h> The 15-Minute City in Global Context <p> The 15-minute city represents a shift away from automobile-centric urban development towards neighbourhood-scale accessibility and a polycentric urban form . Rooted in Moreno 's theory of " chrono-urbanism , " the concept emphasises reducing travel time rather than physical distance , alongside promoting mixed-use neighbourhoods where daily needs are met locally . In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic , the 15-minute city gained prominence as cities sought to reduce long commutes and reinforce local resilience . <p> Paris has emerged as the flagship example of this approach . Under Mayor Anne Hidalgo , the city has pursued extensive pedestrianisation , expanded cycling infrastructure , repurposed schoolyards as public spaces , restricted polluting vehicles , and supported local commerce through regulatory and financial interventions . Similar principles have informed Melbourne 's " 20-minute neighbourhoods " policy and Portland 's " Healthy Connected Neighbourhood Strategy " , both aimed at reducing car dependence and strengthening local social and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pandemic , the 15-minute city gained prominence as cities sought to reduce long commutes and reinforce local resilience . <p> These initiatives are driven by shared objectives : lowering emissions , improving public health , and revitalising neighbourhood economies . Yet even among these global frontrunners , the model has attracted significant critique . Urban economist Alain Bertaud argues that metropolitan systems are fundamentally shaped by labour markets rather than neighbourhood amenities , and that no large city can realistically ensure that most residents work within a 15-minute radius of their homes . This critique shifts the debate from neighbourhood design to the structural organisation of urban economies . <h> Indian Cities : Compact but Unequal <p> On the surface , Indian cities appear well-suited to the 15-minute framework . High-density neighbourhoods , mixed land use , and widespread informal services ensure that daily necessities such as groceries , pharmacies , repair services , and schools are often accessible within walking distance . Street vendors and home-based enterprises further reduce the need for long trips , reinforcing neighbourhood-level convenience . <p> However , proximity in Indian cities often masks profound @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unevenly distributed and overstretched , government schools vary sharply in infrastructure and learning outcomes , and access to recreational or green spaces remains limited in low-income areas . For instance , in Madhya Pradesh , fewer than 1 percent of government schools have digital libraries , while access to smart classrooms remains below 12 percent . These realities underscore the limits of proximity in the absence of quality . Pedestrian infrastructure is similarly inadequate , with footpaths frequently encroached upon , discontinuous , or unsafe . <p> More critically , residential proximity to daily amenities does little to address access to employment . Economic activity in Indian cities is concentrated in a limited number of business districts , while housing continues to sprawl across metropolitan regions . Although public transport connects these areas , it is often unreliable , unsafe , or inaccessible , leading to long and exhausting commutes . As urbanist Alain Bertaud notes , labour markets require scale and diversity -- conditions that inevitably generate cross-city travel . <h> The Labour Market Problem <p> The most fundamental limitation of the 15-minute city model lies in its approach @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ integrated labour markets that allow firms to access talent and workers to access diverse opportunities . Neighbourhood-level proximity does not resolve this challenge . On the contrary , proximity-based planning risks constraining labour markets by implicitly assuming that people should work near home , rather than ensuring efficient access to citywide opportunities . <p> Other scholars argue that an overemphasis on walkability can undermine the role of public transport , while sociologically , the model risks producing inward-looking neighbourhoods that limit broader urban interaction . Even Paris , often cited as the model 's most successful example , does not enable most residents to access workplaces within a 15-minute radius of their homes . Its economic geography remains regionally integrated , with commute times extending well beyond neighbourhood boundaries . <p> Proximity-based planning risks constraining labour markets by implicitly assuming that people should work near home , rather than ensuring efficient access to citywide opportunities . <p> In India , these contradictions are magnified . Employment clusters such as Gurugram , Bengaluru 's Whitefield , and Mumbai 's BKC -- Fort corridor lead to long commutes for workers unable to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in Indian cities stands at 59 minutes , with women spending even longer due to trip-chaining associated with care responsibilities . Meanwhile , nearly 43 percent of Indian cities lack universally accessible footpaths , severely limiting safe walking as a viable option . <p> As a result , the benefits of the 15-minute city accrue disproportionately to affluent , centrally located residents who already enjoy high-quality services and flexible work arrangements . For the majority , the model functions less as a planning solution and more as an elitist abstraction that risks reinforcing , rather than reducing , spatial inequality . <h> Policy Directions for India <p> For Indian cities , a more realistic approach is to shift the focus from neighbourhood self-sufficiency to metropolitan accessibility . This requires decentralising employment through multiple job centres , while ensuring strong , affordable , and reliable public transport connections across the urban region . <p> Improving the quality , not merely the proximity , of essential services is equally critical . Informal economies , which already play a central role in neighbourhood accessibility , must be formally recognised within planning frameworks rather @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , particularly in low-income areas , are essential to make walking a dignified option rather than a necessity borne of exclusion . <p> The 15-minute city offers a valuable reminder that neighbourhood-level accessibility matters , but it can not substitute for the deeper structural reforms that Indian cities require . <p> Time-based accessibility metrics can be useful if applied pragmatically . Instead of assuming that people can live close to work , urban policy must acknowledge long commutes as a structural reality and focus on reducing their social , economic , and gendered costs . <h> Conclusion <p> The 15-minute city offers a valuable reminder that neighbourhood-level accessibility matters , but it can not substitute for the deeper structural reforms that Indian cities require . The everyday convenience of dense urban neighbourhoods does little to address unequal access to jobs , quality public services , and reliable transport . <p> The objective should not be to create self-contained neighbourhoods , but to ensure that all residents , regardless of where they live , can access the full scale of urban opportunity . Without confronting labour market concentration , housing affordability @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a proximity myth : compelling in theory , but exclusionary in practice , revealing a sharp contrast between the model 's promise and lived reality . <p> Ruchita Bansal is an urban planner and founder of SheCity India , focusing on inclusive , gender-responsive urbanism and the political economy of Indian cities .

@@135965654 <h> The Unheard Outcry of Manipur : An Essay on Hoihnu Hauzel 's ' Stories The Fire Could Not Burn ' <p> A state is not defined by those who govern it or by its formal ties with the central authority . It is defined by its people , their lived realities , the conditions they endure , and the circumstances that shape their everyday lives . In this sense , Jammu &amp; Kashmir is often described as a ' critical state ' , not merely for its geopolitical position but for the way its functioning is deeply controlled by the centre , largely through military presence , with little space for meaningful dialogue . <p> Such control has done little to bridge the distance between Kashmiris and the rest of the country . Instead , a dominant narrative has taken root , one that casts Jammu &amp; Kashmir as a breeding ground of terrorism and its people as disloyal , even celebratory of India 's defeats . This perception has been strengthened over time by external conflicts , particularly Pakistan 's interventions , as well as by India 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ political engagement . <p> Key moments , such as the unresolved question of the plebiscite and the abrogation of Article 370 without consulting the people of the state , have deepened this sense of alienation . In many ways , this reflects a recurring history , when aspirations for autonomy or independence of the people of Jammu &amp; Kashmir during and after the partition were overshadowed by the competing interests of two nations , each seeking to contain the region within its own political framework . <p> When it comes to Manipur , a similar condition has been allowed to grow , shaped by successive governments , and pushed to an extreme under the present regime . The difference , however , lies in visibility . Unlike Kashmir , a North-Eastern state like Manipur remains largely absent from the concerns of mainstream India . Its suffering unfolds quietly , receiving little sustained attention . This neglect is evident in the way the ongoing violence , often described as an ethnic conflict between the Kuki-Zomi/Mizo communities and the Meiteis , has been treated . <p> Credit : The New York Times @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ even as it continues , the crisis of Manipur has struggled to find consistent space in mainstream media narratives . The absence is not merely journalistic . It is also political . Even the Prime Minister Narendra Modi , has not visited the state during this prolonged period of unrest . This silence becomes more striking given that the state leadership , including Nongthombam Biren Singh and Yumnam Khemchand Singh , belong to the same ruling party , the Bharatiya Janata Party , and is drawn from the Meitei community , one of the principal groups involved in the conflict . In such a situation , the absence of dialogue and attention only deepens the sense of distance , leaving the crisis to persist in the margins of national consciousness . <p> Hoihnu Hauzel 's Stories the Fire Could Not Burn : A Personal Account of the Manipur Crisis : 2023-25 , does not attempt to position itself within the familiar frameworks of political analysis or journalistic reporting of the Manipur conflict . It refuses the distance that such modes or professions often demand . Instead , this work of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ encounter here is not documentation of the state politics , but a lived testimony and an urgent , unfiltered outcry chiselled by Hauzel 's own proximity to violence and loss . <p> Hauzel writes as someone who has witnessed , in immediate and unsettling ways , how linguistic , ethnic and communal identity can become the basis for brutality . Her narratives are not structured around statistics or official accounts , but around people or individuals whose lives have been irreversibly altered by the state . In choosing to orient these personal stories towards the readers , she draws attention to the fragility of human existence within conflict , where the loss of a home is inseparable from the loss of memory , belonging , and safety . <p> There is also a conscious insistence in her work on recording what might otherwise be dismissed . Individual suffering , she suggests , is often rendered invisible unless it is expressed with a force that demands acknowledgement . The ache that runs through her writing becomes a form of resistance , something that can not be substituted by policy language or @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ intensity that gives her account its ethical weight . <p> At the same time , the book does not shy away from confronting the asymmetries within the conflict . It is navigated towards the unequal distribution of power , suggesting that certain communities bear a disproportionate burden of violence and displacement . In doing so , Hauzel underscores a difficult but necessary truth which is , that in any conflict , naming the structures and agents of oppression is essential , even when such naming unsettles dominant narratives or political constructs and decorum of the nation . <p> Her voice remains firmly personal , grounded in experience rather than mediated interpretation . This makes her account resistant to appropriation . It neither can be polished into neutrality , nor redefined to fit the demands of national image makers . Any attempt to do so would risk erasing the very pain it seeks to convey . In this sense , misdirecting readers by dilution of the conflict 's objective and narrative in the name of balance , decorum , or political convenience , especially at a time when such notions themselves @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ carry the pain of losing the people they loved , resources they lived on and places they inhabited . <p> In the preface of this book , Hauzel confronts , with clarity and defiance , the charge of bias . She acknowledges that some may call her account biased and leaves room for that , for what is often dismissed as bias is , in truth , an urgent need to speak for those whose suffering remains unseen within dominant narratives . In this assertion , she reframes bias not as distortion , but as a necessary act of witnessing . <p> This need arises from the larger indifference that shapes how much of India perceives Manipur and , more broadly , the North-East . Prejudice often enters quietly but firmly , through the casual racism that reduces people to their physical features , making them feel like outsiders . Through the policing of food habits , where what one eats becomes a marker of impurity , the rest of the India excludes them on a personal level . And through a deeper ignorance that treats the region as distant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rest of the country through the narrow stretch known as the Siliguri Corridor , often called the ' Chicken 's Neck ' , a fact that itself becomes a metaphor for its fragile inclusion within the national imagination . <p> This exclusion is not only social but also political and historical . The long enforcement of the Armed Forces ( Special Powers ) Act ( AFSPA ) in Manipur , which has structurally defined the everyday life under militarization , has rarely received any sustained national concern . Acts of resistance too , have often been overlooked , such as the protest of the Meira Paibis , who , in an extraordinary moment of defiance , stripped themselves to challenge the violence and impunity of military power . Even in the present , reports of humiliation and brutality of men and women publicly stripped , beaten , and killed , struggle to receive the attention they demand . <p> Meira Paibis ; Credit : India Today <p> To deepen this narrative of exclusion , Hauzel recalls an incident that unsettles even her own sense of grief , making her struggle @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Letminthang , a Kuki man employed in the Income Tax Department , whose death was marked not only by brutality but by spectacle . He was dragged through the streets , stabbed , beaten with rods , and forced into acts of humiliation against his own community . And when he was already at the edge of death , the mob chose to burn his body by pouring petrol over him , turning this entire act violence into a public statement . <p> Hauzel reflects that what happened to Letminthang was not merely a killing . It was a message that 's inscribed in violence , intended to erase not just a person , but an identity , a community , a name . In recounting this , her writing moves beyond mourning into a sharper recognition of what such acts signify within a larger pattern of conflict . That conflict , she writes , is neither sudden nor isolated . Its roots stretch back to the years following independence , shaped by years of tensions between communities . Within Manipur , the Meitei community , including Meitei Hindus and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the valley , while tribal communities such as the Kuki-Zomi/Mizo and the Naga populations have largely inhabited the hills . <p> Hauzel points to the way certain narratives have been constructed and circulated , particularly the claim that tribal communities occupy 90% of Manipur . While it is true that a large portion of the state is covered by hills , she notes that this geography is frequently misunderstood or misrepresented . Much of this terrain is not uniformly habitable , and the realities of land , access , and settlement are far more complex than such claims suggest . Yet , both the state and central authorities have often failed to address or clarify these nuances , allowing oversimplified narratives to harden into sources of resentment and division . <p> There are reasons why such crucial realities remain ignored . Beneath the surface of conflict lies an economic motive , one that 's tethered to land , resources and control . The push for ' development ' , often shaped by capitalist interests and supported by dominant groups within Manipur , increasingly turns toward the exploitation of natural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inhabited by the tribal communities . <p> In this context , divisive narratives do not emerge accidentally . They serve a purpose or an objective . By portraying hill communities , particularly the Kuki-Zomi/Mizo groups , as occupying disproportionate space , a justification is created for intervention , displacement , and eventual control . As these narratives circulate , they enable both the state and the dominant sections of society to legitimise the gradual erosion of minority settlements while larger economic interests move in to claim land and resources . What develops then is an alignment between the capitalists and the ones who dominate the state and this particular alignment is symbiotic by nature . <p> At the same time , the realities of life in the hills complicate this picture . Limited infrastructure , lack of access to education , healthcare , and economic opportunities compel many from these communities to move toward the plains . The plains , particularly Imphal , become necessary spaces for survival , not sites of encroachment . Yet , this movement is reframed within a different narrative , one that suggests that the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Meiteis from their own land and rights . It is a propagandist tool that is soaked in hatred . <p> Such a narrative , which is repeated and reinforced constantly , leads to the transformation of anxiety into hostility . It produces a sense of threatened ownership among the majority even when the movement of people is driven by necessity of individual development rather than territorial expansion . But to fulfil the interest of the majority , the violence that erupted in Manipur was a way to reclaim what does not belong to a single community . It was an assertive move to control the state in presence of a political regime which has always supported the Hindutva school of division . <p> In the opening chapter , That Dark Night , Hauzel brings together the lived experiences of the Kuki-Zomi/Mizo community with a wider political critique . She narrates the suffering of her own family alongside that of other affected households , but does not allow these stories to remain merely personal . Instead , she places them within a larger structure of state action , showing how policies @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and often worsened , the conditions of minority communities in Manipur . Although many of these developments were documented in national level newspapers , Hauzel suggests that the dominant public discourse has consistently flattened or ignored the complex realities of North-East India . <p> One of the most striking examples she discusses is the decision taken on 14 April 2023 , when the Manipur government approved the construction of 188 religious structures across the state . Notably , all of these were Hindu temples . This move appears deeply disproportionate when placed against the demographic composition of the region . As per the 2011 census , a significant portion of Manipur 's population belongs to minority communities , including the Kuki-Zomi/Mizo tribes , many of whom are Christian . The implementation of this decision was not merely symbolic . It took a material and confrontational form , as churches were demolished using JCB bulldozers . These actions were met with strong resistance from Kuki organizations , who viewed them as direct attacks on their faith and identity . But the message was loud and clear . Under the rule @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ who are mostly Meitei Hindus , are going to benefit and faith here will play a big role in fuelling this divisive narrative . <p> Alongside this , Hauzel traces the emergence of a powerful and troubling narrative , in which the Kuki community is encroaching upon and ' taking over ' land in Manipur . This narrative , she argues , has been instrumental in legitimizing state-led eviction drives . One such case is the eviction of K. Songjang village . Here , older legal frameworks , particularly those related to forest protection introduced after 1972 , were brought back into focus . These laws enabled the state to classify lands inhabited by Kuki-Zomi/Mizo communities as reserved or protected forests , thereby rendering long-standing settlements as illegal ones in administrative terms . <p> The situation became even more precarious in 2015 , when the Union Ministry of Environment , Forest and Climate Change identified forty-eight additional villages as eco-sensitive zones . The implication was that these areas could be transformed into wildlife sanctuaries , further displacing indigenous populations . For the Kuki community , such measures were not just @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ loss of ancestral land , traditional rights , and homes . But it was a calculated move by the people in power , who are Meiteis , to take control of not only Manipur but also those who live in the circle of being in minority . <p> Unsurprisingly , these developments sparked protests . Kuki chieftains and community leaders openly opposed what they saw as unjust and unlawful policies . They argued that such decisions were made without proper consultation and disproportionately targeted tribal populations . Hauzel underscores that the tension reached a critical point on 20 February 2023 after the eviction of the K. Songjang village . On that day , state authorities arrived with six JCB bulldozers and forcefully evicted sixteen Kuki-Zomi/Mizo households . The operation , carried out under the justification of clearing encroachment on protected forest land , was marked by aggression and violence . It left behind not only destroyed homes but also a deep sense of insecurity and dispossession . The protests still remain unheard and , for the mainstream India , the rights of the majority became primary than the insecurity of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Manipur <p> The violence and ethnic tensions in Manipur , Hauzel reminds us , are not sudden or without history . What unfolded in recent years is rooted in older cracks , long defined by questions of identity , land and political recognition . Yet , the immediate trigger for the prolonged civil unrest , she notes , was the solidarity march organized by the All-Tribal Students ' Union of Manipur ( ATSUM ) . The march was a response to the demand by the Meitei community for Scheduled Tribe ( ST ) status , a classification originally meant to safeguard historically marginalized tribal groups who lack equal access to resources and opportunities . Hauzel presents this demand as deeply contentious , especially when extended to a community perceived to already possess relative social , economic , and political advantages . <p> Solidarity March by All Tribal Students ' Union of Manipur <p> The protest , held in Lamka town of Churachandpur , began as a peaceful assertion of dissent . But , as Hauzel carefully traces , that fragile peace soon gave way to spiralling violence . Within @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lost , and over 70,000 people , predominantly from the Kuki-Zomi/Mizo communities were displaced from their homes . What began as a political disagreement soon turned into a humanitarian catastrophe , reshaping the landscape of everyday life in the region . <p> Hauzel strengthens her account by recording the testimony of witnesses , one of whom recalls that it felt as though the Meiteis had come prepared . This sense of premeditation can be found throughout her narrative . From the targeting of symbolic structures such as the Kuki Anglo War Memorial Gate to the systematic destruction of churches belonging to the Kuki-Zomi/Mizo community , the violence appeared neither random nor spontaneous . Instead , it was planned and coordinated . Equally disturbing , she observes , was the apparent inaction or absolute surrender of police forces and those in positions of authority , who failed to intervene meaningfully as the attacks unfolded . <p> The violence , however , is not only described at the level of collective trauma . Hauzel also brings it painfully close to her own family and self . She recounts how one of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ family 's brickfield . This was not just a site of economic activity but a space tied to memory of a Manipur which she grew up in . The brickfield provided employment to many , and its destruction affected not only her family but also those who depended on it . In Hauzel 's telling , this moment becomes deeply personal when the loss of property merged with the loss of a sense of belonging , and the rupture of a past that once felt stable and peaceful . <p> Hauzel 's narrative does not reduce the conflict to a uniform story of violence . She carefully acknowledges that , even in the midst of chaos , there were Meitei families who helped those fleeing from the mobs , offering shelter and guidance to them in whatever way possible . Some officials , too , acted with urgency and conscience , choosing to move vulnerable families to safer places without waiting for formal authorization . These moments of humanity can not overshadow the larger narrative of brutality , reminding the reader that compassion did persist , albeit for a brief @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ such acts , however meaningful , could not outweigh the scale and intensity of the violence that unfolded . A few individuals could not undo what a larger , organized force inflicted upon communities that were already vulnerable which held people with limited resources , no alternative homeland , and little institutional protection even when they participated in the electoral system of the state of Manipur . The imbalance of power becomes starkly visible in her account , as those who were attacked had neither the means to resist nor the assurance of safety . <p> She turns to the example of Paite Veng , a prominent settlement of the Paite community , to illustrate how targeted and systematic the violence appeared . The attack on this locality did not emerge in isolation . Rather , it was preceded by a government order issued in April 2023 . According to Hauzel , three churches , each with histories spanning over fifty years , were suddenly declared ' unauthorized ' and marked for demolition on the grounds that they stood on government land . This decision was abrupt and unsettling and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ precarious atmosphere that seemed to anticipate further conflict . <p> What followed , Hauzel suggests , bore the marks of coordinated attack rather than spontaneity . The assault on Paite Veng and its churches appeared organized , with a striking level of precision in its execution . Notably , while homes belonging to the Kuki-Zomi/Mizo community were attacked and set ablaze , Meitei households in the same area were left untouched . To Hauzel , this selective destruction indicates that the attackers were not acting blindly . They seemed to know exactly which properties to target . The pattern of violence thus reinforces her broader argument that these events were not random outbreaks of anger but carried elements of planning and intent . <p> Hauzel , while writing about the incident in Paite Veng , raises many difficult and unsettling questions about the role of state authority . The sequence of administrative decisions followed by targeted violence creates , in her view , was an impression of complicity or , at the very least , a failure of accountability . Through this , she underscores that when power , policy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ heavily by those already living on the margins . <p> It is important for readers to move beyond the political framework of the conflict and confront its deeply human cost . Hauzel urges us to recognize what violence meant at a personal level , how people were forced to witness the killing of their loved ones , the destruction of their homes , and the violation of their dignity in public . These were not distant events but intimate ruptures , where memory , identity , and belonging were violently reshaped for their own future . The past itself was targeted , as if erasing it could compel people to accept an imposed and newly constructed present . <p> Through her documentation , especially the story of her niece , alongside testimonies from other eyewitnesses , Hauzel reveals a version of Manipur that remains largely absent from official narratives . It is a Manipur that many will not encounter in textbooks or state-sanctioned historical documents in the future . She suggests that this absence is not accidental , but part of a broader tendency of those in power to suppress @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ from confronting state failures . <p> In this sense , the book becomes more than a personal account and transforms into a vital archive . What begins as individual testimonies acquires collective significance , preserving fragments of truth that might otherwise be erased . Hauzel 's work stands as a reminder that when institutions fail to record honestly , personal narratives often become the only means through which reality survives . Her reflections also point to a larger pattern in the writing of history itself . History , she suggests , is often defined and distorted by those who hold power . Whether one looks at events like the American Civil War , the Spanish Civil War , or even more recent episodes of unrest such as the 2020 Delhi riots , the narratives that reach the public are frequently contested , selective , and at times deliberately altered . What is presented as ' history ' may obscure as much as it reveals . <p> For Hauzel , then , the responsibility shifts to push the readers to question , to investigate , and to listen closely to voices @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these voices that one can begin to understand what truly happened , who suffered , who wielded power , and how violence was justified or concealed by the dominant groups . In preserving these testimonies , her work resists erasure and insists on a more honest , if uncomfortable , engagement with the horrific past , which is still the present since Manipur is still facing unrests in several places . <p> Displacement , Hauzel suggests , may seem like an escape from immediate violence , but it carries a quiet and enduring cost . To leave is not simply to move from one place to another . It is to abandon everything that defines one 's identity , home , memory , community , and belonging . For the Kuki people who managed to flee in order to survive , survival itself came at the price of rupture of their own self . They were forced to leave behind not only their houses and land , but also the emotional and cultural worlds that defined them as individuals and as part of a larger community . <p> The displaced @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ neighbouring states such as Assam and Mizoram . These places offered shelter and relative safety yet they remained in unfamiliar terrains . The displaced lived in a state of convolution where they were physically removed from violence , yet emotionally tethered to it . News of continuing unrest kept reaching them , keeping their fear alive and preventing any sense of stability , even with a sense of protection . In this suspended existence , they waited for intervention , for justice , for a return that seemed increasingly uncertain . <p> Hauzel portrays this waiting as deeply painful , especially in the face of what she sees as prolonged inaction . For over two years , the crisis persisted without meaningful resolution which left the state effectively isolated . She suggests that this absence of decisive intervention was not merely a failure , but something more troubling . It was an indifference , or even a political calculation , where unrest served certain interests by diverting attention and enabling other forms of control . <p> At the same time , she notes that the violence did not go entirely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ what was happening , drawing attention to the scale of suffering . Yet , in her account , such criticism did not translate into protection of those who were exiled from their very state . Instead , the situation was navigated towards a larger ideological project , arguing that the marginalization of the Kuki community is tied to an attempt to redefine the social and political fabric of Manipur in a particular direction . With a Hindu-dominated Meitei population , the dream of having a Hindu Rashtra will strengthen for the ruling government . <p> As global conflicts unfold , such as the ongoing tensions involving Iran , Israel , and the United States , we are reminded of how deeply violence is mediated through social media . Hauzel reflects on this unsettling reality that social media often turns suffering into a vicious spectacle , drawing viewers through graphic imagery that provokes empathy , outrage , and , at times , even financial engagement . In this digital economy of attention , pain becomes visible only when it is dramatized . <p> Yet , she also acknowledges a paradox . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ silence . She points out that while graphic representations of violence helped draw national attention , they also carried a heavy emotional burden for those who had already endured displacement and trauma . For survivors , these circulating images were not distant realities but painful reminders of what they had lost and escaped . At the same time , she turns a critical eye toward mainstream media . According to her , many media houses hesitated to fully report on the violence in Manipur . She suggests several reasons for this silence , first being the political context of a state governed by the Bharatiya Janata Party , second being the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and finally , the risks faced by journalists and sympathizers who attempted to present an honest account . In such an environment , truth itself becomes precarious . For this very reason , Hauzel puts a very important question before the readers , what is the purpose of life , if being authentically oneself can summon such hatred ? <p> Stories the Fire Could Not Burn : A Personal Account of the Manipur Crisis : 2023-25 ultimately moves beyond viewing the events in Manipur as just another episode of political unrest . Instead , Hauzel frames it as something more fundamental and troubling . She suggests that the violence was not merely about power struggles , but about systematically redefining the social fabric of the state by targeting the minority in ways that resemble ethnic cleansing rather than any conventional conflict . At its core , however , the book remains deeply personal . It is anchored in love for a homeland that is rapidly transforming in the presence of hatred and hegemony . Through Hauzel 's eyes , we witness not only the physical destruction of places and communities @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' itself . @@135981156 <h> A land that floats , a deer that ' dances ' : Inside world 's only floating national park , Keibul Lamjao in Manipur <p> IMPHAL : Keibul Lamjao National Park -- the world 's only floating national park -- floats delicately on the southern expanse of Loktak Lake in Manipur . Here , the very ground beneath your feet is alive , swaying with thick , buoyant mats of vegetation , soil , and organic matter known as phumdis . It is a place where nature has rewritten its rules , creating a fragile , floating kingdom . Amid this ethereal landscape roams the Sangai , Manipur 's " dancing deer , " whose steps across the floating meadows are as graceful as they are fleeting . Once thought lost to the world , these creatures embody a story of survival , resilience , and the tenuous thread that connects life to the unique rhythms of this watery wilderness . For nearly two decades thereafter , the animal faded from public and administrative attention . However , a turning point came during an aerial survey conducted between 1974 and 1975 , when a small population of approximately fourteen individuals was rediscovered within the floating marshes of Keibul Lamjao . <p> Its rediscovery in Keibul Lamjao by environmentalist E.P . Gee sparked renewed conservation efforts . From a mere 14 individuals in 1975 , the population rose to 155 in 1995 and further to 260 by 2016 . Known as the " dancing deer " for its delicate gait across the floating phumdis , the Sangai 's survival remains inseparable from the health and stability of these unique floating meadows . <p> Following this rediscovery , the government of Manipur and the government of India declared the area a national park in 1977 under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 . Principal chief conservator of forests , Manipur , Anurag Bajpai told TOI , " this legal protection was crucial and notification @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strategy . " According to Bajpai , the Sangai is not just a species but " a culturally rooted animal that has adapted to this habitat over thousands of years , " reflecting a deep relationship between the landscape and the people of Manipur . <p> The Floating Phumdis : Habitat Of " Dancing Deer " The defining feature of the park lies in its floating ecosystem , which form the very ground on which the Sangai survives . Phumdis are not merely patches of vegetation but complex , living structures formed over long periods through the accumulation of plant material , soil , and nutrients . Their formation begins with aquatic vegetation such as azolla and other lower plants . Over hundreds and even thousands of years , these materials consolidate into thick , buoyant masses capable of supporting large animals . For the Sangai , the phumdis serve as habitat , grazing ground , and breeding site . The grasses that grow on them provide essential nutrition throughout the year.Bajpai describes their formation as a slow , natural process . " It takes years together , even thousands @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . " Equally important is the natural cycle of phumdis . The PCCF explains that " the phumdi has to go down to the bottom of the lake , collect nutrients , and then come up , " a process essential for maintaining its health . However , this cycle has been disrupted by the Loktak Hydroelectric Project , which keeps water levels artificially stable . " For the sustainability of phumdi , we want pulsating water levels , " he notes , identifying this as a key ecological challenge . <p> Active Habitat Management And Wildlife ProtectionSince the park 's notification , conservation has focused on managing habitat , protecting wildlife , and balancing ecological pressures . Bajpai likens conservation to maintaining a home : " When you stay at your home , you clean it , repair it , improve it . Similarly , for an animal , its habitat must be maintained . " This includes ensuring adequate food , space , and protection from both natural predators and human interference.Forest Department efforts extend to active habitat management . Phumdis are sometimes transported from other parts of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ area and stability . Bajpai explains , " We bring phumdi from other parts of the lake , tie it with the existing one to increase stability and area . " <p> Vegetation is regularly monitored to ensure that adequate food resources are available for the Sangai throughout the year . Fire management is another crucial aspect , particularly during the dry season when forest fires can spread rapidly across the floating vegetation . Fire lines are created and maintained to prevent the spread of such fires , and emergency measures are taken when necessary to safeguard wildlife , he added.The challenges within the park are not limited to habitat alone . The presence of other species creates ecological competition and predation risks . Bajpai points out that hog deer compete with Sangai for food , while wild boars and pythons pose threats , particularly to fawns . " Area is limited , " he stresses , highlighting the importance of managing carrying capacity within the ecosystem . <p> Community Involvement And Future Conservation StrategiesEqually important is the role of local communities in the conservation process . @@135995201 <h> Energy News Monitor Volume XXII , Issue 24&amp;25 <h> Published on Apr 04 , 2026 <h> Quick Notes <h> Energy Security : The Scramble for Molecules <p> Unlike the 1970s oil shocks , which were largely limited to a single commodity - oil - the 2022 and 2026 energy crises were simultaneous shocks across coal , oil , and natural gas and that too at a time when the global economy was far more interconnected and therefore more vulnerable . The 2026 energy crisis , which is threatening economies with sharp price increases and volume shortages , is also raising questions over some of the accepted narratives in the energy sector . The idea that hydrocarbons and hydrocarbon-producing nations are no longer central to energy security was one of the accepted narratives . The rationale was that the world was awash with surplus oil and gas and that supply disruptions would be compensated immediately . A subsidiary narrative was that shale oil production in the US would make up for any loss in global oil supply , as the United States ( US ) , the world 's largest oil producer , had taken the role of Saudi Arabia as swing producer . The blockage of the Strait of Hormuz , through which 25 percent of seaborne oil trade , 20 percent of petroleum products and 20 percent of LNG ( liquefied natural gas ) trade passes , has shown that hydrocarbon producers in West Asia and the hydrocarbons they produce and export remain central to energy security . The US role as swing producer has not materialised . The private shale oil producers in the US are more attuned to private profit generation through capital discipline than to the production of public goods such as energy security . <p> Fossil fuels supplied approximately 86.5 percent of global primary energy in 2024 and continue to dominate electricity generation , transport , and heavy industry . When Russian pipeline gas deliveries to Europe fell after the crisis in Ukraine , Europe replaced pipeline gas with LNG . Natural gas prices in Europe reached their highest point in September 2022 at roughly twenty-five times the price two years ago . Coal acted as the residual balancing plant when natural gas became prohibitively expensive . Oil , natural gas and coal were fungible enough to allow rapid , if imperfect , substitution among themselves when supply was constrained . <p> Pipeline natural gas and LNG are chemically the same , primarily methane -- but differ in logistics and marginal cost . Pipeline gas is cheap to transport once the infrastructure is built , but the geography of intercontinental pipelines exposes them to geopolitical changes . LNG requires liquefaction , which is energy and cost-intensive , with an internal energy penalty of about 10 percent ; it requires specialised tankers and regasification terminals , which carry energy and cost penalties . In the three years ending in 2025 , Europe built more than 50 billion cubic meters ( bcm ) of additional LNG import capacity , converting what was a regional market into a globally contestable one . Dual-fuel boilers and power-generating capacity improved energy security . Many European facilities can switch between gas and oil distillates within hours ; some Asian utilities can switch between LNG and coal . <p> Inter-fuel substitution is clearly visible in the ongoing crisis over Iran . With LNG supply from Qatar reduced , Asian economies South Korea , Bangladesh and Indonesia are increasing coal-fired power generation . Oil is harder to substitute in transport without investment in assets such as electric vehicles ( EVs ) , but the supply shock is reinforcing the case for diesel and residual-fuel-oil stockpiles at strategic hubs . <p> Fundamental engineering realities underpin the versatility of fossil fuels . A barrel of oil or a tonne of coal has higher volumetric and gravimetric energy density than lithium-ion batteries or hydrogen . Natural-gas combined-cycle plants can ramp from zero to full load in minutes and provide the inertia and frequency response to the grid that inverter-based renewables struggle to replicate without massive overbuild and storage . Coal-fired stations increase emissions but offer months of on-site stockpiling -- insurance that intermittent solar and wind can not provide against geopolitical or weather shocks . <p> These substitutions are not costless . They increase emissions , strain supply chains , and introduce price volatility that is transmitted through marginal-cost electricity pricing . This means the most expensive fossil fuel unit often sets the clearing price . Yet inter-fuel substitution will prevent far worse outcomes such as industrial shutdowns , widespread blackouts , and social unrest . The fungibility of fossil fuel infrastructure , including but not limited to ports , rail systems , pipelines , tankers and refineries , allows markets to reoptimize faster than alternatives . <p> For India , along with other economies , energy security now ranks alongside decarbonization as a policy priority . Strategic reserves , diversified import portfolios , and dual-fuel capability are viewed as national-defence investments . Substitution capacity within fossil fuels is offering indispensable time . LNG terminals are serving as flexible assets now , and they can eventually carry bio-LNG or synthetic methane . As proposed in the Indian budget for 2026-27 , coal plants can be retrofitted with carbon capture if economics become favourable . The premature retirement of these energy assets risks stranding operational flexibility when shocks occur . <p> The Indian government allocated INR58.76 billion in the 2025 -- 26 Union Budget for the construction and filling of SPRs ( strategic petroleum reserves ) . Spending on construction and operations of the SPR is estimated to be about 14-15 percent of the allocated budget . At full capacity of about 5.33 million metric tonnes , the SPRs can provide about 9.5 days of net import cover . However , due to incomplete filling of SPRs , the effective strategic buffer is estimated to be lower . With the price of the Indian basket of crude at about US$125/barrel in March 2026 and increased subsidy commitments , India is likely to face macroeconomic challenges . <p> The call to accelerate the energy transition to insulate India from fossil fuel supply and price shocks is repeated in every energy forum . But fossil fuel supply shocks influence the pace of the energy transition . The correlation between fossil fuel prices and renewable energy costs , driven by the energy-intensive nature of industrial manufacturing and global logistics , is a reality . While renewables provide zero marginal cost energy ( free solar and wind ) , their upfront capital expenditure is highly sensitive to the cost of oil , gas , and coal . The production of " green " infrastructure relies on three primary fossil-fuel-dependent channels . The production of steel for wind turbine towers , aluminium for solar frames , and polysilicon for solar cells requires large quantities of heat and electricity . Steel production typically relies on coking coal , while aluminium and polysilicon refining are often powered by natural gas or coal-fired grids . When these fuel prices spike , as they are now , the cost of these raw materials rises proportionally . Energy can account for up to 40 percent of the total production cost for base metals . Carbon fibre and epoxy resins used in wind turbine blades , as well as the plastic back sheets and ethylene-vinyl acetate ( EVA ) encapsulants used to protect solar panels , are directly derived from petrochemicals . As crude oil prices increase , the cost of these specialised polymers also increases . <p> In addition , global supply chains for renewables are incredibly transport-heavy . Moving large wind blades or thousands of solar modules requires significant maritime and heavy-truck transport , both of which are dependent on diesel and bunker fuel prices . Additionally , the heavy machinery used for onsite construction -- such as cranes and excavators -- operates almost exclusively on liquid petroleum fuels , adding a hidden energy premium to every new megawatt of capacity . The scramble for molecules , if replaced by the electrons from renewables , could potentially increase not only the scramble for materials but also the scramble for fossil fuel molecules . <h> Monthly News Commentary : OIL <h> LPG Import Basket Diversifies <h> India <p> LPG <p> The government is planning to change how the LPG ( liquefied petroleum gas ) subsidies are calculated after India increased its oil imports from the US ( United States ) . Till December FY 2026 , CIL has despatched about 375 million tonnes ( MT ) of coal through rail mode which was sampled by TPSAs .
