@@136246717 <p> This paper re-reads these ancient moral imperatives through the lens of contemporary neuroscience , evolutionary biology , sociology , and peace studies . It contends that the Decalogue is not a relic of ancient tribal theocracy but a " beta code " for human liberation -- a cognitive , social , and spiritual architecture designed to prevent ontological violence and foster genuine human flourishing . By integrating scriptural analysis with the latest findings of Robert Sapolsky , Martha Nussbaum , Johan Galtung , Amartya Sen , and others , this paper advances a humanistic synthesis capable of grounding arguments against war-mongers , religious fanatics , and political fundamentalists on foundations that are simultaneously ancient and scientifically robust . The Decalogue , properly understood , is not the property of any single religion ; it is the moral grammar of a species that wishes to survive . <p> The Moral Structure of a World in Crisis <p> In the spring of 2026 , the world presents a spectacle that would have been recognisable to the authors of the Book of Exodus . Nations are arrayed against nations ; civilians flee burning cities ; oil fields are seized under the cover of military action ; women are raped as a systematic instrument of war ; and the chambers of diplomacy echo with sophisticated lies dressed in the language of international law . The technological apparatus of civilisation -- satellites , algorithms , financial instruments , nuclear arsenals -- is immeasurably more advanced than anything the ancient world imagined . And yet the moral failures on display are identical to those that prompted the most ancient law codes in human history . <p> This paper contends that this coincidence is not accidental . The moral pathologies that drive modern warfare -- the idolatry of national power , the dehumanisation of the enemy , the unchecked appetite for resources , the instrumentalisation of women 's bodies as weapons , the weaponisation of truth itself -- are precisely the pathologies that the Decalogue , the Quranic ethical catalogue , and the teachings of Jesus were designed to diagnose and cure . These are not three separate moral systems competing for adherents . They are three articulations of the same deep structure of human social requirements , each adapted to a specific historical and cultural context , but each pointing toward the same horizon : a world free from ontological violence , structured by justice , and animated by the love of the neighbour . <p> The central argument of this work is deceptively simple . Human beings are , in the language of evolutionary biology , obligate social animals . Our survival as a species depends upon our ability to cooperate in groups , and sustained cooperation is impossible without trust . Trust , in turn , is impossible in the absence of the moral commitments encoded in the Decalogue : do not kill your fellow human beings arbitrarily ; do not steal what belongs to others ; do not bear false witness ; do not consume your neighbours with covetous desire . These are not arbitrary divine commands ; they are , as neuroscience now confirms , the formalised conditions of our biological flourishing ( Sapolsky , p.24 ) . When nations violate them on a mass scale -- as happens in every modern war -- they are not merely sinning in a theological sense ; they are attacking the biological and psychological infrastructure of the human species itself . <p> This paper proceeds in ten substantive sections . It begins with the foundational preamble of the Decalogue , which locates all moral law within the prior act of liberation . It then addresses , in turn , the specific contemporary crises of killing and warfare , resource looting and oil theft , sexual violence against women , and deception in international affairs . It examines religious fanaticism and fundamentalism as a modern form of the idolatry condemned in the first three commandments . It reviews the scientific evidence for the biology of violence and the biology of peace . It reflects on the Sabbath principle as a pointer toward ecological and human sustainability . It concludes with a vision of justice , peace , and flourishing drawn from the synthesis of the ancient moral codes and the most current findings of the human sciences . <p> A note on method : this paper reads the Decalogue and its Quranic and Christian parallels through what may be termed a " Quranic humanistic lens . " This does not mean that the analysis is confined to Islamic thought , nor that it is in any way dismissive of other traditions . Rather , it means that the specific Quranic articulations of the moral imperatives -- with their emphasis on Adl ( justice ) , Ihsan ( excellence ) , Mizan ( balance ) , and Karama ( inherent dignity ) -- provide a unique and inclusive framework for the synthesis attempted here . The Quran speaks to the entirety of humanity as " the children of Adam " ( 17:70 ) , and it is in that universal spirit that this work proceeds . <p> The Exodus Preamble : Liberation as the Prerequisite of Law <p> The Decalogue does not begin with a command . It begins with an announcement : " I am the Lord your God , who brought you out of the land of Egypt , out of the house of slavery " ( Exod. 20.2 ) . This preamble is the hermeneutical key to the entire document . Before the first imperative is issued , a prior act of liberation is declared . The law is not imposed upon slaves ; it is offered to free people . This sequencing is theologically and politically decisive . <p> In the ancient world , Pharaoh 's Egypt was the paradigmatic extraction state . Slaves were human beings reduced entirely to their productive utility . There was no Sabbath under Pharaoh ; there was only the quota of bricks . The Decalogue , as the theologian Walter Brueggemann has argued , is at its very foundation an " anti-Pharaoh " document -- a constitution for a community that has been liberated from the logic of pure extraction and must now learn to live otherwise ( Brueggemann , p.3 ) . The moral law is the social form that liberated life takes when it refuses to replicate the systems of its oppressors . <p> This preamble has direct and urgent implications for contemporary warfare . Every modern war is , in some fundamental sense , a reassertion of Pharaoh 's logic . It is the attempt by one power to reduce another people -- and other people 's land , resources , and women -- to instruments of its own will . When a nation invades another to seize its oil , it is re-enacting the slavery of Egypt in a modern key : it is saying that the people of that land are not subjects with inalienable rights but objects whose resources can be expropriated by superior force . When armies systematically rape women in occupied territories , they are asserting precisely the logic of the slave-master : that the bodies of the conquered are the property of the conqueror . The Decalogue was written against this logic . Its preamble insists that human beings are , first and foremost , liberated subjects -- never the property of another power . <p> The Quranic resonance is profound . The Quranic ethical catalogue in Q.6:151-153 and 17:23-39 presents moral imperatives as " Hikmah " -- Wisdom -- and as the " Straight Path " for a community emerging from the chaos and tribalism of the pre-Islamic era . Just as the Biblical Decalogue follows the escape from bondage , the Quranic mandates offer a framework for maintaining the integrity of a community that has moved beyond the " Jahiliyyah " -- the era of ignorance and tribal violence . In both traditions , the moral law is the scaffold upon which a liberated society is built . Without it , freedom degenerates either into the anarchy of " every man for himself " or into the tyranny of " the strongest man for all . " <p> The implications for contemporary political philosophy are clear . No state , however powerful , can claim the right to re-impose the logic of Pharaoh upon other peoples . International law , at its best , is an attempt to codify this Exodus preamble in secular terms : it asserts that the sovereignty of every people is prior to the power of any invading force , just as the freedom of the liberated community is prior to the commands of the law . When war-mongers invoke " national interest " or " security imperatives " to justify conquest , they are speaking the language of Pharaoh . The Decalogue answers them from its very first line . <p> Against Killing : The Sanctity of Life in an Age of Perpetual War <p> The Sixth Commandment -- " You shall not murder " ( Exodus 20.13 ) -- is the bedrock of any viable social contract . Yet it is also the commandment most systematically violated by the modern state in its conduct of war . The history of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries is , in significant part , a history of the industrialisation of killing : from the trenches of the Somme to the gas chambers of Auschwitz , from the atomic obliteration of Hiroshima to the drone strikes of the global war on terror , from the machetes of Rwanda to the barrel bombs of Syria . What makes this history so morally instructive -- and so tragic -- is that virtually every episode of mass killing has been accompanied by sophisticated moral justifications : self-defence , civilisational necessity , religious duty , ethnic survival , pre-emptive security . The perpetrators of mass violence are almost never cynics . They are , as Robert Sapolsky 's landmark work demonstrates , human beings whose capacity for dehumanisation has been activated by the particular combination of ideology , fear , and social pressure ( Sapolsky , p.490 ) . <p> The Quranic elaboration of this commandment is among the most powerful statements of the sanctity of life in any religious literature . The Quran states : " Whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption in the land -- it is as if he had slain all of mankind . And whoever saves one -- it is as if he had saved all of mankind " ( 5:32 ) . This is not merely a moral sentiment ; it is an ontological claim . Each human life is presented as a microcosm of the whole -- a unique and irreplaceable expression of the human family . To destroy it is not merely to harm an individual ; it is to rupture the entire fabric of the species . <p> This Quranic universalisation of the soul is the definitive refutation of the logic of dehumanisation . Every act of mass killing in history has been preceded by a process of symbolic degradation : the victim group is labelled as less than human -- as " cockroaches , " as " vermin , " as " infidels , " as " collateral damage . " The anthropologist Michael Taussig has called this " the magic of the state " -- the ability of political authority to transform persons into objects through the alchemy of language ( Quoted in Sapolsky , p.555 ) . The Decalogue 's Sixth Commandment and the Quranic elaboration of 5:32 are a direct counter-magic : they re-person the victim , insisting that every life destroyed is a universe destroyed . <p> Contemporary neuroscience provides a compelling biological corroboration . Sapolsky 's research demonstrates that the human capacity for empathy is biologically real and neurologically instantiated . The mirror neuron system allows human beings to simulate the pain and experience of others within their own nervous systems ( Sapolsky , p.575 ) . Crucially , however , this empathic capacity is profoundly susceptible to manipulation . When a person is categorised as " Other " -- as a member of a different ethnic , religious , or national group -- the empathic response is diminished or suppressed altogether . The ideological work of war is precisely the work of suppressing empathy : of making it cognitively and emotionally possible to kill people whom , in any other context , one would recognise as persons . The moral counter-technology of the Sixth Commandment is the insistence that this suppression is illegitimate : the neighbour , however defined , remains a person , and persons may not be killed . <p> Jesus radicalises this commandment by tracing the root of murder to its psychological antecedent : " You have heard that it was said to those of old , You shall not murder ... But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgement " ( Matt. 5.21-22 ) . This is a remarkable anticipatory insight into the social psychology of violence . The neurobiological chain from angry contempt to physical aggression is well-documented in the literature ( Goleman , p.59 ) . Jesus targets the chain at its earliest link . A civilisation that wishes to prevent war must cultivate the internal dispositions that make war psychologically impossible : the recognition of the full humanity of every person , the discipline of empathy over contempt , and the practice of conflict resolution through dialogue rather than domination . <p> For contemporary war-mongers , religious or secular , the answer of the Decalogue and its parallels is unambiguous : no cause , however sacred it is proclaimed to be , justifies the mass killing of civilians . No oil field , no border dispute , no theological disagreement , no perceived humiliation of national honour , licenses the industrialised destruction of human lives . The Sixth Commandment is absolute in the most humanistic sense of the word : it is grounded not in an arbitrary divine decree but in the biological and ontological reality that every human life is a universe , and its destruction is a crime against the species as a whole . <p> The Plunder of Nations : Oil Theft , Economic Looting , and the Eighth Commandment <p> The Eighth Commandment -- " You shall not steal " ( Exodus 20.15 ) -- has , in the context of modern international relations , an application that its original framers could not have imagined : the systematic theft of an entire nation 's natural resources under the cover of military occupation or economic coercion . In the twenty-first century , the most conspicuous form of large-scale theft is the seizure or exploitation of oil -- the fossil fuel that underwrites modern industrial civilisation and that has , accordingly , become the most fought-over commodity in human history . The wars in Iraq , Libya , Sudan , and the South China Sea , the geopolitical manoeuvring around the Caspian Basin and the Gulf states , the sanctions regimes designed to exclude certain nations from the revenues of their own resources -- all of these are expressions , in one form or another , of the violation of the Eighth Commandment at the level of the international order . <p> The Quranic parallel is remarkably specific . In the Quran , the ethical mandate extends from the personal prohibition of theft to an explicit requirement of institutional integrity in the distribution of resources : " And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best ... and give full measure and weight in justice " ( 6:152 ) . The " orphan " in the ancient context was the paradigmatic non-person -- someone with legal rights but no power to enforce them . In the modern context , the " orphan " is the citizen of a nation whose sovereignty is nominal but whose resources are extracted by more powerful actors through the mechanisms of debt , military occupation , asymmetric trade agreements , or outright conquest . The Quranic insistence on " full measure and weight in justice " is a demand for institutional integrity in the international economic order . <p> Amartya Sen 's " Capabilities Approach " provides the contemporary philosophical framework for understanding why resource theft is a moral catastrophe of the first order ( Sen , p.3 ) . Sen argues that economic development is , at its core , a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy -- their ability to live long and healthy lives , to access education , to participate in political life , and to exercise the basic functions of human dignity . When a nation 's oil or mineral wealth is seized by an occupying power or extracted through a system of exploitative contracts , the consequence is not merely an accounting loss . It is the destruction of the capability base of an entire generation . The schools that could have been built , the hospitals that could have been staffed , the public infrastructure that could have been maintained -- all of these are the victims of resource theft . It is a form of slow-motion killing as lethal as the Sixth Commandment 's prohibition of murder , differing only in the time scale of its violence . <p> David Graeber 's study of the history of debt illuminates a related mechanism of structural theft : the use of international financial instruments -- debt , interest , structural adjustment conditionality -- to extract value from poorer nations and transfer it to wealthier ones ( Graeber , p.12 ) . This is the contemporary equivalent of the Quranic prohibition of Riba ( usury ) -- the categorical condemnation of systems that allow capital to multiply without genuine productive contribution , while placing the burden of compounding repayment upon the debtor . When an international financial institution imposes austerity conditions upon a nation in exchange for emergency loans , compelling it to sell its natural assets at distressed prices , it is committing a form of institutional usury that the Quranic ethical system identifies as a profound violation of justice . <p> The neuro-economics of fairness provides the scientific counterpart to this moral argument . Research using the " Ultimatum Game " -- a laboratory paradigm in which subjects can accept or reject a proposed division of resources -- consistently demonstrates that human beings have an evolved " Fairness Instinct . " When the division is perceived as grossly unjust , subjects reject the offer even at personal cost , triggering a response in the anterior insula -- the region of the brain associated with the experience of disgust ( Sapolsky , p.490 ) . This biological response to unfairness is the evolutionary substrate of the moral sense : it is the neurological echo of the Eighth Commandment , a deep somatic protest against the violation of fair measure . It suggests that the outrage of nations subjected to resource imperialism is not merely political ; it is a biological response to the violation of a universal human norm . <p> The Quranic concept of Khilafa ( Stewardship ) provides the positive corollary to the prohibition of theft . If the Earth and its resources are held in trust for the whole of humanity -- including future generations -- then no single state or corporate entity can claim absolute ownership of a nation 's subsoil assets . The human being is a " Khalifa " -- a trustee -- not an owner whose rights of extraction and destruction are unlimited . This principle of stewardship over ownership is the ethical foundation for the emerging body of international environmental law , which increasingly recognises that the resources of the natural world are a " common heritage of mankind " rather than the private property of whoever happens to have the military power to occupy the terrain above them . <p> Gender Violence , Sacred Dignity , and the Seventh Commandment <p> Among the most ancient and most persistent war crimes is the systematic sexual violation of women by occupying or invading forces . The rape of women in war is not an aberration or an accident of conflict ; it is , as the documentation of the International Criminal Court and the United Nations Security Council resolutions on " Women , Peace and Security " have established , a deliberate weapon of war , a tactic of ethnic cleansing , a mechanism of social domination , and a symbolic assertion of the conqueror 's absolute power over the conquered ( UN Security Council Res. 1325 ) . In Bosnia , Rwanda , the Democratic Republic of Congo , and Iraq , mass sexual violence has been prosecuted -- too rarely , too slowly , and with too few convictions -- as a crime against humanity . It is also , this paper argues , a categorical violation of the Seventh , Fifth , and Sixth Commandments simultaneously : it destroys the person , it desecrates the covenant of bodily integrity , and it murders the dignity that makes human life worth living . <p> The Seventh Commandment -- " You shall not commit adultery " ( Exodus 20.14 ) -- is , in its humanistic reading , a protection of " Relational Integrity " and the " Sanctity of Consent . " Read in the context of wartime sexual violence , it takes on a dimension of terrible urgency . Rape is not adultery in the conventional legal sense ; it is the violent destruction of the very capacity for consensual relationship . A humanistic reading of the Seventh Commandment must therefore encompass the absolute prohibition of all non-consensual sexual acts , since the commandment 's deepest purpose is to protect the " Relational Commons " -- the space of trust and mutual vulnerability in which genuine human bonds are formed . <p> The Quranic parallel is notably preventive : " And do not go near adultery ; indeed , it is an indecency and an evil way " ( 17:32 ) . The phrase " do not go near " establishes a proactive ethics of protection rather than a merely reactive prohibition . In the context of war , " going near adultery " encompasses the entire culture of militarism that treats women 's bodies as spoils of conquest -- the propaganda that dehumanises the enemy 's women , the command cultures that turn a blind eye to sexual violence , the social impunity that makes prosecution rare and conviction rarer still . The Quranic imperative demands that we address these preconditions of violation , not merely the act itself . <p> The Quranic anthropology of the " Single Soul " ( Nafsin Wahidah ) provides the deepest foundation for the moral argument against wartime sexual violence ( Quran 4:1 ) . If all of humanity shares a single creational origin -- if the woman in the occupied territory is , in the most fundamental ontological sense , made of the same substance as the soldier who violates her -- then the act of rape is a violation not merely of another person but of one 's own essential nature . It is a form of ontological self-destruction , a rupture in the " Single Soul " of the species . The Islamic feminist scholar Amina Wadud has argued that this " Tawhidic paradigm " of the Quran demands the absolute equality and dignity of all human beings , and that any claim of the right to dominate or violate another person on the basis of gender , ethnicity , or conquest constitutes a form of Shirk -- the idolatrous elevation of the self over the divine standard of justice ( Wadud , p.34 ) . <p> Contemporary neurobiology confirms the catastrophic and lasting damage of sexual violence . Trauma research documents that the experience of rape -- particularly in the context of war , where it is typically public , repeated , and stripped of any possibility of help -- produces severe and enduring dysregulation of the body 's stress-response systems , including hyperactivation of the amygdala and suppression of prefrontal cortical function ( Sapolsky , p.204 ) . The long-term consequences include post-traumatic stress disorder , chronic depression , social withdrawal , and the transmission of trauma across generations through epigenetic mechanisms . Sexual violence is thus a form of biological warfare : it does not merely harm the individual victim but damages the neurobiological foundations of entire communities , making the intergenerational transmission of the wound a certainty without sustained , expert intervention . <p> Jesus ' interactions with women in the New Testament offer a consistent model of what the " fulfilment " of the Seventh Commandment looks like in practice . When he declines to condemn the woman brought before him by her accusers , he is not condoning the act ; he is refusing to participate in the use of a woman 's body as the site of a political contest between factions of men . He restores her as a subject -- a person with a future -- rather than allowing her to remain an object of male definition . This " radical personalism , " as this paper terms it , is the positive content of the Seventh Commandment 's prohibition : the active recognition of every person 's inviolable subjectivity , which makes sexual violence , in any form , under any pretext , absolutely inadmissible . <p> Deceit in International Affairs : False Witness and the Crisis of Global Trust <p> The Ninth Commandment -- " You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour " ( Exodus . 20.16 ) -- has , in the twenty-first century , assumed a geopolitical importance that its ancient framers could not have anticipated . We live in an era of systematic state-sponsored deception : manufactured pretexts for war , fabricated intelligence reports , algorithmic disinformation campaigns , " deepfake " video evidence , diplomatic bad faith , and the routine exploitation of international legal language to disguise aggressive intent . The " weapons of mass destruction " that justified the invasion of Iraq in 2003 , the " humanitarian intervention " narratives that have masked resource seizure in various theatres of conflict , the elaborate infrastructure of " active measures " by which powerful states subvert the democratic processes of their neighbours -- these are all , in the language of the Decalogue , " false witness . " They are systematic lies told at the highest level of the international order , with consequences measured in hundreds of thousands of deaths . <p> The legal philosopher John Rawls argued that the stability of a just society depends on " Public Reason " -- the ability of citizens to debate and decide on the basis of shared facts and logical inferences ( Rawls , p.212 ) . Without a shared commitment to the Ninth Commandment , public reason collapses into " tribal rhetoric , " where the goal of speech is not to report reality but to signal loyalty , manufacture consent , or destroy the credibility of the opponent . This is the condition of much international discourse in 2026 : a state of " epistemic war " in which the first casualty is not merely truth in the abstract but the specific human lives that depend on accurate information for their survival . <p> Beyond its legal implications , the Ninth Commandment acts as a fundamental ethical bulwark against the architecture of hatred campaigns by demanding absolute integrity in both public and private discourse . While often interpreted within a narrow judicial context , the prohibition of false witness is more broadly a mandate against any misrepresentation of reality that harms another . It targets the " engines " of hatred -- backbiting , tale-bearing , and the intentional spreading of damaging information -- which rely on what may be termed " selective reasoning . " <p> In the lead-up to conflict , propagandists employ selective reasoning through three primary mechanisms : first , they isolate and exaggerate , highlighting negative hearsay while suppressing broader context ; second , they generalize accusations , applying an individual 's perceived fault to an entire ethnic or national group ; and third , they invent motives , attributing malevolence to neutral actions to " demonize " the neighbour . <p> The Decalogue directly combats these mechanisms through the " Whole Truth " Principle . By forbidding the circulation of false reports , the commandment implies an affirmative duty to speak the truth in its entirety , thereby destroying the fragmented context necessary for hate speech . This is deeply linked to the " Love Commandment " ; because slander is inherently unloving , the Ninth Commandment serves as a covenantal obligation to protect the neighbour 's dignity . <p> Furthermore , this prohibition serves a crucial sociological function by preventing the " Bandwagon Effect . " It requires individuals to resist joining a " multitude to do evil " ( Exodus 23:2 ) or spreading popular but malicious gossip , demanding instead an independent , truth-based judgment . As Proverbs 6:16-19 suggests , the " false witness who breathes out lies " is an abomination not merely because of the damage to reputation , but because such deceit reflects a character antithetical to the Truth . Ultimately , false witness is a corrosive force that dissolves the trust and social fabric essential for any functional society , making its prohibition a prerequisite for peace . <p> The Quranic contribution to this epistemic ethics is , as noted in the introduction , among the most radical in any religious literature . The Quran commands : " O you who believe , stand firm for justice as witnesses for God , even if it be against yourselves , or your parents , or your close relatives " ( 4:135 ) . This is the definitive refutation of the tribalism that underlies most geopolitical deception . The requirement to testify truthfully even against oneself -- even against one 's own nation , one 's own government , one 's own side in a conflict -- is an extraordinarily demanding standard . It is , however , the only standard that makes international law genuinely possible rather than merely performative . A world in which states can routinely lie at the Security Council , in which intelligence agencies can fabricate the evidence for war , in which military communiques bear no systematic relationship to events on the ground , is a world in which the Rule of Law has become a charade . <p> The Quran adds a personal dimension of remarkable specificity : " And when you speak , be just , even if it be against a relative " ( 6:152 ) . The demand for impartial truth -- truth that overrides loyalty to the tribe , the party , the nation , the religion -- is the foundational principle not only of the scientific method and the rule of law but of civilised international relations . Every diplomat who deliberately misrepresents facts at a negotiating table , every head of state who knowingly fabricates a casus belli , every propagandist who manufactures stories of the enemy 's atrocities to justify the commission of one 's own -- each is violating this commandment . And the consequences , as the history of the past century demonstrates with terrible clarity , are not abstract . They are measured in the bodies of the dead . <p> Jesus distilled the Ninth Commandment into a principle of character rather than merely of conduct : " Let your Yes be Yes and your No be No " ( Matt. 5.37 ) . The implication is that truth-telling is not a matter of contractual obligation or legal constraint ; it is an expression of the coherence of the self . A person whose inner reality matches their outer speech -- whose " witness " is reliable because they have made the alignment of truth and language a matter of personal integrity -- is the human foundation upon which any just social order must be built . At the level of international affairs , this translates into the requirement for " epistemic institutions " -- free press , independent courts , genuine multilateral oversight , algorithmic transparency -- that make it structurally difficult to bear false witness at scale . <p> The cognitive science of deception confirms the social costs of normalised lying . Leon Festinger 's research on cognitive dissonance shows that the maintenance of systematic deception requires enormous psychological resources and produces chronic stress ( Festinger , p.42 ) . Robert Putnam 's research on social capital demonstrates that societies with high levels of honesty and transparency consistently outperform those characterised by pervasive distrust in every measure of human flourishing -- economic productivity , democratic stability , public health , and subjective well-being ( Putnam , p.135 ) . When states normalise deception in their international conduct , they do not merely harm their adversaries ; they degrade the epistemic environment upon which their own citizens ' capacity for self-governance depends . The Ninth Commandment is not only a moral requirement ; it is a public health mandate for the species . <p> Idolatry as Violence : Religious Fanaticism , Fundamentalism , and the First Tablet <p> Among the most urgent applications of the Decalogue to the contemporary world is its first and foundational cluster of commandments -- the prohibition of idolatry and the demand for exclusive loyalty to the transcendent source of justice . For the purposes of this paper , " idolatry " is understood not in the narrowly theological sense of worshipping stone statues but in its broader humanistic sense : the elevation of any finite , human-made reality -- a nation , a race , an ethnicity , an interpretation of scripture , a political ideology , a charismatic leader -- to the status of an absolute , which then acquires the right to determine who lives and who dies . <p> In this humanistic sense , violent religious fundamentalism is itself a form of idolatry . It is the elevation of a particular community 's interpretation of the divine will to the status of an unchallengeable absolute , which then licenses the killing of those who disagree . The scholar Khaled Abou El Fadl has argued , in his account of the " Great Theft " of Islam from its humanistic interpreters , that the violent extremism associated with certain strands of contemporary Islamism is not an authentic expression of the Quranic tradition but a profound distortion of it -- precisely because it commits the sin of Shirk by placing the absolute authority of the state , the group , or the leader where only the transcendent can legitimately stand ( Abou El Fadl , p.82 ) . The same critique applies , with appropriate variations , to Christian fundamentalism , Hindu nationalism , Buddhist chauvinism , and every other form of religious violence : each represents the usurpation of the divine by the human . <p> The First Commandment -- " You shall have no other gods before me " ( Exodus 20.3 ) -- is , in its humanistic reading , a declaration of independence for the human conscience from all totalising human authority . By asserting that only the transcendent source of justice and mercy is ultimate , the Decalogue effectively strips every human institution , every political party , every religious community , every charismatic leader of the right to claim absolute obedience . Theodor Adorno 's research on the " Authoritarian Personality " demonstrates that human beings are biologically prone to leader-worship , particularly in times of social crisis ( Adorno , p.154 ) . The First Commandment is a cognitive vaccine against this tendency . It tells us that no human being is worthy of the absolute devotion that fanatics give to their leaders and their movements . <p> The Second Commandment -- the prohibition of graven images -- extends this critique to conceptual idols . In the modern world , the most dangerous conceptual idols are not carved from wood or stone but from ideology . The nation-state , when it claims that its interests override the universal requirements of justice , becomes an idol . The " pure " ethnic or religious community , when it claims that its survival justifies the elimination of the impure , becomes an idol . The " true " interpretation of scripture , when it claims to possess a certainty so absolute that it licenses violence against those who interpret differently , becomes an idol . Jonathan Haidt 's research on moral psychology demonstrates that human beings are natural-born " groupish " creatures who find it neurologically easy to sanctify their own group and demonise others ( Haidt , p.262 ) . The Second Commandment is the counter-move : a standing injunction against the sacralisation of the in-group and the demonisation of the out-group . <p> The Third Commandment -- the prohibition of taking the divine name " in vain " -- is the specific prohibition against weaponising the sacred . When religious leaders invoke the name of God to justify mass violence , to sanction the rape of enemy women , to bless the seizure of another people 's oil , or to legitimise diplomatic deception , they are not exercising religious authority ; they are committing what this commandment identifies as the most fundamental form of blasphemy . The Quranic parallel -- the condemnation of those who " sell God 's signs for a small price " ( 2:41 ) -- makes explicit that the misuse of sacred language for political or violent ends is a betrayal of the very tradition in the name of which it is perpetrated . A true humanistic monotheism , as both the Decalogue and the Quran conceive it , can not be weaponised : The God who commands " do not murder " can not simultaneously command murder , and any tradition that claims otherwise has replaced the living transcendent with a human-made idol wearing the disguise of the divine . <p> For the war-monger who claims religious sanction , for the fundamentalist who kills in the name of the sacred , for the fanatic who demands absolute loyalty to the group , the message of the Decalogue 's First Tablet is simple and unambiguous : you have made your cause your god . You have committed Shirk . You are not fighting for the divine ; you are fighting for your own image of the divine , which is precisely what the First , Second , and Third Commandments forbid . And because you have replaced the transcendent source of justice and mercy with a human-made absolute , you have also lost the only standard by which your violence could ever be justified -- because the transcendent source of justice does not justify the murder of the innocent , the theft of the weak , or the rape of the powerless . It forbids them , absolutely , in the very commands that inaugurate moral life . <p> The Neuroscience of Violence and the Biology of Peace <p> One of the most significant developments in the scientific literature of the past three decades is the convergence of neuroscience , evolutionary biology , and social psychology around a single , profoundly hopeful conclusion : human beings are not , at their deepest biological level , primarily aggressive . We are , as the evolutionary biologists Samuel Bowles and Herbert Gintis have demonstrated , a " Cooperative Species " whose survival has depended , for the overwhelming majority of our evolutionary history , on our ability to build and sustain high-trust social groups ( Bowles and Gintis , p.15 ) . The capacity for violence is real and is not to be minimised ; but it is , as Sapolsky 's comprehensive review of the neurobiological evidence demonstrates , always a contextually triggered exception to a more fundamental orientation toward pro-sociality ( Sapolsky , p.24 ) . <p> This scientific insight has direct and important implications for the argument of this paper . If the Decalogue and its Quranic and Christian parallels encode the conditions under which human pro-sociality flourishes -- if they are , in biological terms , formalisations of the cooperative norms that allowed our species to survive and evolve -- then the violation of these commandments by war-mongers and religious extremists is not merely a moral failure . It is a biological attack on the species ' own survival mechanisms . War , resource theft , sexual violence , and deception are not expressions of deep human nature ; they are pathological departures from it , made possible by the specific social and ideological conditions that the Decalogue was designed to prevent . <p> The neurobiological evidence for the " Love Commandment " of Jesus is particularly striking . Paul Zak 's research into the hormone oxytocin has demonstrated that it is the biological substrate of trust , generosity , and social bonding ( Zak , p.52 ) . Acts of kindness -- what the Quran calls Ihsan , " doing what is beautiful " -- trigger oxytocin release , which in turn reduces the amygdala 's fear response and promotes the prosocial behaviours that sustain high-trust societies . Conversely , conditions of systemic injustice , violence , and deception suppress oxytocin production and elevate cortisol -- the stress hormone associated with the " fight or flight " response -- creating a neurobiological environment in which violence becomes more likely , trust becomes harder to sustain , and the social fabric continues to fray . In short : The Decalogue is a programme for optimising the neurochemistry of civilisation . Following its precepts is , in a very literal sense , good for our brains . <p> Johan Galtung 's distinction between " Negative Peace " ( the mere absence of direct violence ) and " Positive Peace " ( the presence of social justice , institutional integrity , and horizontal empathy ) provides the peace studies framework that gives scientific content to the vision of " flourishing " that animates this paper ( Galtung , p.167 ) . Negative Peace is what the Second Tablet of the Decalogue , taken in isolation , produces : a world in which people refrain from killing and stealing each other . Positive Peace is what the Love Commandment of Jesus and the Quranic Ihsan principle add : a world in which people actively invest in one another 's flourishing , building the social capital that makes genuine , durable , and just peace possible . <p> The Richard Wilkinson and Kate Pickett study of the relationship between inequality and social outcomes provides perhaps the most powerful empirical demonstration of why the economic commandments of the Decalogue -- against theft , against the exploitation of the orphan , against usury -- are prerequisites not merely for justice but for the basic public health of a society . Comparing data across twenty-three developed nations , Wilkinson and Pickett demonstrate that more unequal societies consistently have higher rates of violence , lower life expectancy , higher rates of mental illness , lower levels of trust , and weaker educational outcomes -- regardless of their average level of wealth ( Wilkinson and Pickett 20 ) . Equality is not a luxury ; it is a biological necessity . And the moral architecture that the Decalogue provides -- fair measure , protection of the orphan , prohibition of theft -- is the institutional form that biological necessity takes when a society chooses to live by the grain of its own nature . <p> The Sabbath Principle : Sustainability , Rest , and Ecological Justice <p> The Fourth Commandment -- " Remember the Sabbath day , to keep it holy " ( Exod. 20.8 ) -- is , at first glance , the most distant from the contemporary crises of war , oil theft , sexual violence , and diplomatic deception . In fact , as this section argues , it is intimately connected to all of them . The Sabbath is the commandment that regulates the human appetite for extraction . It is the institutionalised " pause " -- the weekly reminder that neither the human person nor the Earth is a machine whose sole purpose is production . It is the prototype of all sustainable ethics . <p> Brueggemann 's reading of the Sabbath as a form of resistance against the " Pharaoh " of the market -- the ideology of infinite growth and endless productivity -- is directly relevant to the crisis of resource imperialism ( Brueggemann , p.3 ) . The wars fought over oil and minerals are , at their deepest level , wars fought by societies that have never internalised the Sabbath principle : societies that treat the Earth and its peoples as " standing reserves " of productive resources , to be extracted without limit and without rest . The Sabbath says : stop . The Earth is not yours to consume without end . The people of the land you covet are not yours to exploit . There is a rhythm to the world that must be respected , and the refusal to respect it -- the insistence on extraction without pause , production without rest , accumulation without restraint -- is not merely morally wrong ; it is , as contemporary climate science demonstrates , biologically lethal . <p> The Quranic parallel -- the concept of Mizan ( Balance ) and the warning against Fasad ( Corruption in the Earth ) -- provides the ecological theology that makes the Sabbath principle cosmically significant . The Quran declares that the balance of the natural order is a divine trust : " And the heaven He raised and imposed the balance , that you do not transgress within the balance " ( 55:7-8 ) . The industrial plunder of the Earth 's fossil fuels , forests , soils , and biodiversity is , in this framework , a form of cosmic transgression -- a violation of the Mizan that sustains all life . Johan Rockstrom 's " Planetary Boundaries " framework provides the scientific quantification of this ancient insight : there are nine " safe operating spaces " for humanity , and we have already breached several of them ( Rockstrom , p.472 ) . The Sabbath is the weekly enactment of the recognition that these boundaries exist and must be honoured . <p> In terms of human well-being , the Sabbath principle aligns with contemporary research in sleep science , chronobiology , and occupational health . Matthew Walker 's research demonstrates that chronic sleep deprivation -- the biological equivalent of a violated Sabbath -- leads to neurocognitive decline , emotional dysregulation , cardiovascular disease , and suppressed immune function ( Walker , p.112 ) . Human beings are not machines . We require periods of genuine rest and non-utility to integrate our experiences , repair our bodies , and renew our capacity for creative and compassionate engagement with the world . The Sabbath is the moral institutionalisation of this biological requirement : a weekly declaration that the human person 's value is not contingent upon their productive output , and that the Earth 's integrity is not contingent upon our willingness to exploit it . <p> Love as the Fulfilment of the Law : From Prohibition to Possibility <p> The Ten Commandments , as this paper has argued , are a defensive perimeter against the primary vectors of social destruction : violence , theft , sexual violation , deception , and covetousness . But if moral life were to stop at the level of prohibition , it would produce a society that is at best " stable " -- one in which people refrain from harming one another but do not actively invest in one another 's flourishing . The prophetic traditions of all three Abrahamic faiths converge on the insight that the law , in its fullest form , is not merely a set of prohibitions but the expression of a deeper positive imperative : the imperative to love . <p> Jesus ' synthesis of the entire Law into two commandments -- " Love the Lord your God with all your heart ... and love your neighbour as yourself " ( Matt. 22.37-40 ) -- is the most radical compression of the moral code in the history of ethics . It does not abolish the Decalogue ; it fulfils it by identifying the internal disposition from which all genuine compliance with the law flows . If I truly love my neighbour as myself , I will not kill them , steal from them , lie about them , or covet what they have . The law becomes not a constraint imposed from without but an expression of who I have become within . <p> The Quranic concept of Ihsan -- " doing what is beautiful , " the ethics of excellence that goes beyond the minimum required by justice -- is the Islamic articulation of the same positive imperative . The Quran presents a tripartite social mandate : " Indeed , God orders justice ( Adl ) , and kindness ( Ihsan ) , and giving to relatives " ( 16:90 ) . Adl is the floor : the minimum requirement of fairness and non-harm . Ihsan is the ceiling : the commitment to active , generous , creative investment in the flourishing of the other . A society that operates only at the level of justice is a litigious society ; a society that operates at the level of Ihsan is a flourishing one . The positive psychology research of Martin Seligman confirms that " prosocial behaviour " -- acting for the benefit of others without direct personal reward -- is the primary predictor of long-term life satisfaction ( Seligman , p.180 ) . <p> Isaiah Berlin 's distinction between " Negative Liberty " ( freedom from interference ) and " Positive Liberty " ( freedom to realise one 's potential ) provides the political philosophy framework for this transition ( Berlin , p.121 ) . The Ten Commandments , in their prohibitive form , deliver Negative Liberty : they clear the ground of the primary obstacles to human flourishing . The Love Commandment and the principle of Ihsan deliver Positive Liberty : they provide the energy , the motivation , and the vision that allow human potential to unfold in the cleared ground . Liberation is not merely the absence of oppression ; it is the presence of genuine possibility . And genuine possibility requires not only that we stop doing the things that harm our neighbours but that we start doing the things that help them flourish . <p> Martha Nussbaum 's " Capabilities Approach " -- the philosophical framework that measures justice by the actual ability of persons to function and flourish across a range of central human capabilities -- provides the contemporary humanistic expression of this vision ( Nussbaum , p.33 ) . A just society is not merely one in which people are protected from murder , theft , and deception ; it is one in which people have the real capabilities to live long and healthy lives , to access education and meaningful work , to participate in political life , to experience emotional and relational fulfilment , and to exercise the full range of their distinctively human capacities . The Decalogue protects these capabilities from their primary threats . The Love Commandment and Ihsan activate them , sustain them , and invest in their deepest development . <p> Toward a Global Covenant of Justice , Peace , and Flourishing <p> The synthesis of all the foregoing arguments points toward a single , integrated vision : the " Global Covenant of Flourishing " -- a universal social contract grounded in the ancient moral wisdom of the Decalogue and its parallels , validated by the most current findings of the human sciences , and expressed in the institutional forms appropriate to a deeply interconnected world . This covenant is not a utopian dream . It is a biological necessity for a species that has developed the technological power to destroy itself but has not yet developed the moral maturity to prevent doing so . <p> The Quranic declaration that all of humanity has been created from a " Single Soul " ( Nafsin Wahidah ) ( 4:1 ) is the foundational ontological statement of this covenant . It asserts that the person on the other side of the conflict , on the other side of the border , on the other side of the theological dispute , is not a stranger but a member of the same fundamental community of being . This is not a sentimental claim ; it is a biological reality . Genetic science confirms that the human species is , on the relevant timescale , extraordinarily homogeneous : the diversity we observe at the surface level of ethnicity and culture conceals a profound unity at the level of our shared genetic heritage . The " Single Soul " paradigm is , in this sense , good evolutionary biology . <p> In practical terms , the Global Covenant of Flourishing requires the institutionalisation of the moral imperatives this paper has analysed : <p> Against killing and warfare : the reinforcement of international humanitarian law , the consistent prosecution of war crimes in genuinely independent international tribunals , and the sustained diplomatic investment in the resolution of conflicts before they escalate to mass violence . The Sixth Commandment 's prohibition of murder must be given institutional teeth adequate to the scale of contemporary military technology . <p> Against resource theft and economic looting : the reform of the international financial architecture to ensure " full measure and weight in justice " ( Quran 6:152 ) -- transparent contracts , equitable revenue sharing , the cancellation of odious and unjust debts , and the recognition that the natural resources of a people are held in trust for the full development of their capabilities , not for the enrichment of foreign powers or domestic elites . <p> Against the rape of women in war : the consistent and vigorous prosecution of sexual violence as a war crime and a crime against humanity ; the full implementation of the UN Security Council resolutions on Women , Peace and Security ; and the transformation of military command cultures to eliminate the conditions of impunity that make mass sexual violence possible . <p> Against diplomatic deception : the strengthening of the institutions of international transparency -- free press , independent monitoring bodies , open-source intelligence -- and the development of genuinely accountable multilateral mechanisms for the verification of state claims and the enforcement of international commitments . <p> Against religious fanaticism and fundamentalism : not the suppression of religion , but its reclamation from the war-mongers and extremists who have colonised it . The humanistic traditions within every faith -- the tradition of Al-Ghazali and Ibn Rushd in Islam , of Francis of Assisi and Thomas Aquinas in Christianity , of Maimonides and Abraham Joshua Heschel in Judaism -- must be amplified , supported , and given the institutional platforms they need to speak to their communities with the authority of authentic tradition against the distortions of violent extremism . <p> The philosopher Kwame Anthony Appiah 's concept of " Cosmopolitanism " -- the recognition that we have obligations to all human beings , not merely to our fellow citizens -- provides the contemporary philosophical expression of the Quranic " Global Ummah " ( Appiah , p.12 ) . In a world in which climate change , pandemics , and financial instability respect no borders , the " nationalist idolatry " that locates all moral obligation within the boundaries of the nation-state is not merely morally inadequate ; it is biologically dangerous . The destiny of the human species is shared . We will flourish together , as the Quranic single soul working toward a collective Eudaimonia , or we will suffer together the consequences of our collective refusal to do so . <p> The science of cooperation provides the empirical ground for this hope . Robert Axelrod 's landmark study of the " Iterated Prisoner 's Dilemma " demonstrates that in repeated interactions over time , the most successful strategy is not aggressive self-interest but " Tit for Tat with Forgiveness " -- a strategy that begins with cooperation , responds to betrayal in kind , but is always willing to return to cooperation when the other party demonstrates willingness to do the same ( Axelrod 27 ) . This is the scientific counterpart to the Quranic command to " repel evil with that which is better " ( 41:34 ) and to Jesus 's call for reconciliation and forgiveness . The path to durable peace is not the domination of the powerful over the weak ; it is the construction of robust systems of mutual accountability in which cooperation is reliably rewarded and betrayal is reliably discouraged . <p> The Straight Path Forward <p> This paper has argued that the Decalogue -- interpreted through a humanistic lens and read in dialogue with the Quranic ethical corpus and the teachings of Jesus -- provides the most enduring and comprehensive moral argument against the defining crimes of contemporary warfare and international disorder : killing , looting , oil theft , rape , and diplomatic deception . It has further argued that this moral architecture is not merely an ancient religious document but a sophisticated , scientifically validated set of conditions for human biological and social flourishing -- conditions that the latest findings of neuroscience , evolutionary biology , social psychology , and peace studies consistently confirm and elaborate . <p> The war-monger who invaded another nation for its resources has violated the Sixth and Eighth Commandments simultaneously : he has murdered and stolen . The military commander who permits or orders the rape of women has violated the Seventh Commandment and the Quranic principle of Karama -- the inherent dignity of every child of Adam . The diplomat who fabricates the pretexts for war has violated the Ninth Commandment and the Quranic imperative of Qist -- impartial justice even against one 's own side . The religious fanatic who kills in the name of God has violated the First , Second , and Third Commandments simultaneously : he has made his own will into a god , worshipped an idol of his own ideological construction , and taken the name of the divine in the most catastrophic vain possible . The corporate and state actors who plunder the natural resources of weaker nations have violated the Eighth Commandment and the Quranic principle of Khilafa -- the stewardship that we owe to the Earth and to future generations . <p> Against all of these , the Decalogue speaks with an authority that is simultaneously ancient and urgently contemporary . It speaks not as the property of any single religious tradition but as the moral grammar of the species -- the earliest articulation , in the language available to the ancient world , of the conditions under which human beings can live together without destroying one another . It speaks from the Exodus preamble 's insistence that human beings are , first and last , free subjects rather than instruments of another 's will . It speaks from the Quranic single soul 's assertion that every human life is a universe , and its destruction a crime against the whole . It speaks from Jesus 's synthesis of the entire law into the single imperative of love -- love that is not a sentiment but a practice , not a feeling but a discipline , not a private devotion but a public commitment to the flourishing of every neighbour , however near or far . <p> In the year 2026 , the foundations of human liberation are not hidden . They are written in our oldest moral texts , confirmed by our newest scientific findings , and echoed in the deepest biological architecture of our evolved social nature . The question before humanity is not whether we have the moral knowledge to build a just and peaceful world . We do . The question is whether we have the moral will to enact it : to dethrone the idols of national interest , racial supremacy , religious exclusivism , and unchecked greed that demand the sacrifice of our neighbours upon their altars , and to choose instead the " Straight Path " of justice , truth , and love . <p> The Decalogue was given to a community of former slaves as they stood at the threshold of a new existence , free from the logic of Pharaoh for the first time . It was given not as a burden but as a gift : the moral framework within which genuine freedom becomes possible . In 2026 , we stand at a similar threshold . The crises that surround us -- climate collapse , military expansionism , mass sexual violence , information warfare , the rise of authoritarian fanaticism -- are all symptoms of the same underlying failure : the refusal to honour the conditions of our own flourishing . The Decalogue , read humanistically and scientifically , tells us what those conditions are . It remains for us to meet them . The path is straight . The question is whether we will walk it . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> V.A . Mohamad Ashrof is an independent Indian scholar specializing in Islamic humanism . With a deep commitment to advancing Quranic hermeneutics that prioritize human well-being , peace , and progress , his work aims to foster a just society , encourage critical thinking , and promote inclusive discourse and peaceful coexistence . He is dedicated to creating pathways for meaningful social change and intellectual growth through his scholarship . @@136246736 <p> The world is being urbanized at an unprecedented rate . With the rush to smarten up its cities , the cities in the world are at risk of developing fragile infrastructures that work well when temperatures are normal but fail miserably when subjected to climate pressures . Addressing the multifaceted intricacies of climate resilience is crucial in determining the future and sustainability of our cities . The future of cities is not the most connected but most resilient . <p> Introduction : <p> Globally , the urban population has accelerated from 751 million in 1970 to 4.4 billion in 2020 indicating an unprecedented growth and has led to an important disruption towards the urban transformation ( United Nations , 2018 ) . Over 50 percent of the global population currently reside in urban areas and by 2050 the number will hit up to 70 percent ( United Nations , 2019 ) . This paradigm shift called for an immediate action and hence Smart Cities Mission ( SCM ) is an initiative launched in India during 2015 , though this was prevalent in some parts of the globe since 1994 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change with the solution to the congestion in cities , energy usage , and governmental inefficiency . Sustainability is a significant aspect that can not be ignored in any urban environment scenario , specifically in the context of certain limitations it is exposed to ( Bibri , 2019 ) . Digital environments , Internet of Things sensors and artificial intelligence are promising smoother and paved way for more sustainable city living . Smart cities and climate change are holistic by themselves and connected to each other through the common goal of envisaging sustainable modern surroundings . Nevertheless , there is an escalating climate change , which is exposing urban areas to floods , heat waves , air pollution and water crisis . The paradox arises , and the cities that are technologically advanced may be the one that are environmental sensitive . <p> Smartness and vulnerability <p> The past few years have seen the establishment of smart cities in Europe and Asia , as well as in Africa and Latin America . The Smart City model in Barcelona was used as a reference point on a world scale due to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lighting and governance . However , even Barcelona was forced to change its strategy and implement a Climate Emergency Action Plan 2021-2030 , introducing so-called climate shelters , greening , and dual adaptation measures to ensure the safety of the population in the city during extreme heat and floods ( Ajuntament de Barcelona , 2021 ) . Smartness was not enough to be resilient and needed to be climate-adapted . <p> These contradictions are witnessed in the Global South . An example of this is Delhi , in May 2022 it registered record-breaking heat of 49 C despite spending massive amounts of money on digital monitoring systems and transport ( BBC , 2022 ) . High temperatures paralyze the electricity supply and put local population at health risks . The megacity of digital promise Jakarta is literally sinking , by an average of seven centimetres a year , as the land subsides and sea levels rise ( Shatkin , 2019 ) . Its overambitious move to a new smart capital , Nusantara , is indicative of technological ambition as well as the sheer power of the climate reality . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to detect . The investments in infrastructure often focus on monitoring tools , applications , and sensors only , whereas corporeal systems , including stormwater drainage , flood barriers , or green roofs , do not receive adequate investment . The 2015 crippling floods in Chennai unveiled this disparity . Although there was monitoring in place , the submerged city with clogged waterways and poor drainage cost billions of dollars and resulted in widespread social disruption ( Seenirajan et al. , 2017 ) . <p> There is another layer of social inequality . The smart city projects are more likely to end up concentrating the benefits in the richer areas . The disadvantaged groups living in informal quarters are usually out of the focus of the digital platform . The 2018 water crisis in Cape Town , where the town was declared to go without running water on the April 2nd , 2018 , demonstrated the effects of climate shocks in increasing inequality . The rich families invested in their own storage and electronic monitoring , and the poor residents could hardly receive the rationed products ( Enqvist&amp; Ziervogel , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ integration . The IT ministries or urban development authorities tend to spearhead the Smart city programs , whereas climate adaptation is delegated to environment or disaster management departments . The silos in the institution are expensive . <p> Finally , yet importantly , there is the question of data governance . Smart cities generate masses of data , e.g. , on mobility , energy , consumption , and rarely transform into climate resilience dashboards . One remarkable exception is Singapore , which has incorporated risk forecasts and environmental statistics in its Smart Nation ( Woo , 2020 ) . <p> Examples of integration <p> Rotterdam has been the pioneer in the so-called model of Climate Proof which is a mix of smart monitoring and green infrastructure . Its water plazas are used as a common area and also as a temporary reservoir during heavy rains and the underground storage is used to ensure that it does not flood . Such initiatives combine physical resilience initiatives with sensors and predictive models ( van de Ven et al. , 2016 ) . <p> Keeping in mind its intelligent mobility and energy systems @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which integrate digital monitoring and water sensitive design ( Larsen et al. , 2016 ) . In this case , the use of technology is not a goal but a means to build resilience . <p> Innovation has been bottom-up in Jakarta . Social media crowdsourcing to map floods in real-time was used in the Peta Jakarta project to enable the authorities to respond dynamically to the monsoon ( Holderness and Turpin , 2015 ) . Through the connection between citizen involvement and technology , resilience was increased in areas that had less formal infrastructure . <p> Even Japan had to learn disaster . Following the 2011 tsunami , its pilot smart city directly included the element of disaster resilience , meaning that energy networks , residential , and community services would be able to withstand shocks ( Cabinet Office , Japan , 2020 ) . This integration is an appreciation of the fact that , technology that lacks resiliency is partially complete . <p> Policy directions <p> The measures based on connectivity or efficiency alone generate incentives to make superficial investments . To be resilient , indicators ( flood @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ be the centre of smart city ranking and evaluation . <p> Second , there should be redirection of financial flows . Climate-resilient infrastructure should also be a part of the smart city budgets . This bias in the emerging AI ethics framework would have long-term consequences for India and the Global South if it is n't corrected in time . This could be another wave of colonisation and could lead to chaos and disruptions not only in our societies but even in the Western world . <p> In this context , it is important to look at AI ethics through the lens of ' Dharma ' . <p> Though ' Dharma ' is a philosophical framework that encompasses a wide variety of subjects , in the context of AI ethics one can go by the definition provided by Professor Diwakar Nath Acharya at the University of Oxford . In his introduction to the compendium of working and research papers presented at the ' Oxford Dharma Conference ' at ' All Souls @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Etymologically derived from the word dhr , Dharma literally means the one ' that sustains ' . It denotes a universal principle of sustainability that has been recognised , practised , and elaborated within diverse schools of thought in the Indosphere . At its core , the idea of Dharma represents the essential function of upholding order , balance , and integrity within existence and the web of relationships that constitute it . " <p> Framework Gaps <p> According to Patra and Parwani , though AI is a global technology , the ethical frameworks currently shaping its development remain predominantly grounded in post-Enlightenment Western philosophical assumptions , especially individualism , rights-based liberalism , and utilitarian reasoning . While these frameworks have produced valuable insights and regulatory tools , they inadequately address the long-term ethical challenges posed by socially embedded AI systems . <p> Empirical mapping of global AI guidelines reveals that many such principles that are described as " universal " do , in fact , largely reflect the normative vocabulary of Western More Economically Developed Countries ( MEDCs ) . This asymmetry is not just geopolitical ; it shapes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as a moral problem and what solutions are thinkable . <p> If we introduce Dharma as a complementary framework for AI ethics from a Global South perspective , it would contribute to three key shifts : <p> An ' ontological shift ' from the isolated , atomistic individual to the relational self ; a ' teleological shift ' from merely preventing ( non-maleficence ) harm to promoting Yogakshema ( welfare encompassing abhyudaya ( material prosperity ) and nihasreyasa ( ultimate good ) ) ; and a ' methodological shift ' from universal abstraction to context-sensitive judgement guided by desa-kaala-patra ( place-time-agent ) . <p> Risks and Conclusion <p> Patra and Parwani have underlined the threats from a non-Dharmic AI ethics framework , which is currently being pursued . According to them , without deliberate , inclusive , and ethically grounded interventions , AI risks perpetuating existing power asymmetries , eroding trust , and undermining human agency . Conversely , if harnessed responsibly and equitably , AI holds the potential to solve some of humanity 's most pressing challenges -- from climate change modelling and precision medicine to personalised education and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The historical intellectual relationship between the West and the non-West is governed by a binary where the former is considered to be the creator and provider of all rational knowledge , whereas the latter is considered to be the repository of only mystical or spiritual knowledge . This relationship appears to be driving the framing of AI ethics as well . Thus , the universal principles being codified for AI ethics are based on the preferences of the Western world because of their economic and technological hegemony . <p> The integration of Dharma-based principles into the global discourse on AI ethics offers a vital framework that must be integrated with the existing Western framework . It is n't a substitute but must be treated as complementary to address the specific ontological , teleological , and methodological limitations of the prevailing Western paradigm . <p> Advisory Alert:It has come to our attention that certain individuals are representing themselves as affiliates of Moneycontrol and soliciting funds on the false promise of assured returns on their investments . @@136267359 <p> A new report released by the International Labour Organization ( ILO ) calls for strong social protection systems for all type of workers . <p> The report , Universal social protection in changing labour markets : Protecting workers in all types of employment emphasises that reinforcing social protection systems is essential to ensure that all workers , across all types of employment are protected against social risks and able to navigate profound labour market transformations . <p> Social protection , or social security , is defined as the set of policies and programmes designed to reduce and prevent poverty and vulnerability across the life cycle . Social protection includes nine main areas -- child and family benefits , maternity protection , unemployment support , employment injury benefits , sickness benefits , health protection , old-age benefits , disability benefits and survivors ' benefits . <h> What is needed to strengthen social protection systems ? <p> Social protection systems must evolve from merely reducing poverty to actively preventing it , ensuring that individuals are supported before they fall into vulnerability . In a rapidly changing world of work , marked @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these systems has become an urgent priority . To remain effective , social protection must adapt to labour market realities and guarantee universal access to adequate and comprehensive benefits for all workers , including those in temporary , part-time , and self-employed roles . <p> The report highlights encouraging examples from various countries where social insurance has been extended to previously excluded groups , such as workers in agriculture , domestic work , micro- and small enterprises , and complex employment arrangements . Expanding coverage in this way not only improves income security but also promotes fairness and inclusion . Social security contributions in Europe and Central Asia represent more than 27 per cent of total taxation . In Africa , Asia and the Pacific , where they are relatively less important , they still make significant contributions to government revenue . Despite persistent coverage gaps and challenges in extending social insurance to those currently in the informal economy , social insurance contributions have remained a stable source of financing for social protection systems . <p> The social insurance coverage is particularly important for women , as it provides a much greater policy space and potential for broad risk-sharing , redistribution and measures to offset gender inequalities in the labour market . <p> Finally , in light of challenges such as climate change , technological transformation , and demographic shifts , the report underscores the critical role of robust social protection systems in fostering resilience and stability . <p> Social protection systems are key in protecting people and economies from shocks and stresses , and promoting social and economic development , says the report .

@@136278898 <h> Gender Justice is Central to Climate Justice : Interconnections between Climate Change and Gender in India . <p> It has been repeatedly shown through all kinds of studies that South Asia is one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change impacts . India , being the most populous and at a precarious low-medium human development stage , stands at the frontline of the climate crisis . We simultaneously face a multitude of climate change impacts -- intensifying heatwaves , erratic monsoons , floods , droughts , and sea-level rise combined with more frequent and stronger cyclones . Yet , these impacts are not experienced equally . They intersect deeply with existing social inequalities and hierarchies -- especially gender , caste , class , and geography -- creating layered vulnerabilities . <p> In this context , gender justice is not merely a social concern ; it is fundamental to achieving meaningful climate justice in India . <p> 1 . Gendered Climate Vulnerabilities in India : <p> In India , women are disproportionately dependent on direct access to natural resources for both their livelihoods and family care -- whether through @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ low end fisheries , or collecting forest produce . According to multiple studies , a large share of rural women work in climate-sensitive sectors but lack ownership of land and tangible assets . This creates a paradox : high exposure to climate risk but low control over adaptation resources . <p> Heat Stress and Informal Labour : <p> India 's intensifying heatwaves -- especially in regions like Rajasthan , Delhi , Telangana , and Odisha ( now the entire Indi-Gangetic basic is seriously affected ) -- have severe implications for women in informal work . Women working in construction , brick kilns , domestic work , and agriculture often work longer hours in extreme heat , but <p> have limited access to cooling , hydration , or rest spaces . <p> They also face multiple health risks such as dehydration , heat exhaustion , and complications during pregnancy . <p> The legacy of grassroots movements like the Chipko Movement demonstrates how women have long been environmental defenders . <p> At the policy level , global institutions such as UN Women and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change emphasize that women @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are yet to translate these into actionable plans . One of the contributing factors for this is that , in India , women remain underrepresented in formal climate governance and decision making positions . <p> In India , the climate crisis is as much a social crisis as it is an environmental one . Gender shapes who is most affected , who adapts , and who decides . Women -- especially those from marginalized communities , bear disproportionate burdens while also holding key knowledge and leadership potential . <p> A climate response that ignores gender will fail -- not only ethically , but practically . Gender justice is therefore indispensable to climate justice . It ensures that climate action is equitable , inclusive , and transformative -- capable of addressing both ecological sustainability and social justice . <h> Support Countercurrents <p> Countercurrents.org is on annual fundraising drive .
